items.abstract: NPU design-space exploration for LLM inference mainly relies on an expensive simulator that often returns only scalar feedback such as latency and power. Such feedback can rank evaluated configurations, but gives little information for deciding why a configuration is slow or which architecture parameter should be changed next. This limitation is especially severe because prefill and decode workloads can be limited by different resources, including compute throughput and HBM bandwidth. We propose CriticNPU, a sample-efficient DSE framework built around an online-calibrated mechanistic critic for NPU architecture design. The critic uses explicit hardware limits to evaluate NPU configurations: before simulation, it estimates whether a proposed configuration is likely to improve over the current best and filters weak candidates; after simulation, it aggregates operator-level runtimes into prefill/decode bottleneck summaries and predicts the effect of candidate parameter changes. We instantiate the critic with a Roofline-style model that derives compute and memory limits from architecture parameters and calibrates per-operator-type effective limits using simulator observations. And CriticNPU combines this critic with a workload extractor and an architecture planner to propose configurations. Across six LLM workloads and 16 deployment configurations per model, CriticNPU achieves best-or-tied-best latency in 74% of prefill and 87.5% of decode settings while using roughly half the simulator calls of competitive DSE baselines. We conduct extensive ablation studies and detailed analyses to validate the effectiveness of our method from multiple perspectives. Our code is available at https://github.com/bruno686/CriticNPU.

items.title: Jeveration: System One Models Now Generate
items.summary: System One models such as Jev return decisions through fast, parallel prediction. In this paper, we introduce Jeveration, showing that the same decision paradigm can also generate high-quality images in a single forward pass. Jeveration builds on a frozen vision-language model, repurposing its visual-semantic knowledge for holistic image generation. The key challenge is to maintain global consistency. A single…
items.abstract: System One models such as Jev return decisions through fast, parallel prediction. In this paper, we introduce Jeveration, showing that the same decision paradigm can also generate high-quality images in a single forward pass. Jeveration builds on a frozen vision-language model, repurposing its visual-semantic knowledge for holistic image generation. The key challenge is to maintain global consistency. A single prompt admits many valid images, yet parallel predictions must converge on a coherent whole. We therefore condition all positions on a shared random state to coordinate parallel predictions, so that each draw yields a different but coherent image. Since the model tends to ignore this state under direct image supervision, we first learn a distribution over discrete image codes to guide single-pass generation. Beyond text-to-image generation, we further unify image-to-image generation and dense prediction within the same architecture, so that one checkpoint supports all three tasks, each in one forward pass. Experiments show that Jeveration generates a 512x512 image in 78 ms, up to 122x faster than existing unified models, while maintaining competitive image quality and dense prediction performance.

items.title: Game2Player: Scaling Gameplay Experience for Visual Agents through Environment-Player Co-Development
items.summary: Games are a rich testbed for visual agents, demanding perception, long-horizon planning, and precise control. However, collecting human gameplay is costly, and learning from gameplay videos requires inferring missing actions. Existing datasets also cover a limited range of games, often without explicit tasks or verifiable outcomes. To address these gaps, we introduce Game2Player, a framework that co-develops game…
items.abstract: Games are a rich testbed for visual agents, demanding perception, long-horizon planning, and precise control. However, collecting human gameplay is costly, and learning from gameplay videos requires inferring missing actions. Existing datasets also cover a limited range of games, often without explicit tasks or verifiable outcomes. To address these gaps, we introduce Game2Player, a framework that co-develops game environments and players to collect diverse and verifiable gameplay experience at scale. In the Game2Player loop, a Builder agent adapts existing web games, exposes their internal state, and defines tasks with state-based progress measures and success checks. A Coding Player and a VLM Player then attempt the tasks and report problems to the Builder for repair, so that play serves as both environment validation and training data collection. With Game2Player, we build 568 verified web games with 3,436 tasks, collect 15.7K trajectories (307 hours of gameplay), and hold out 50 games as the benchmark PlayerBench. To evaluate the collected experience as training data, we train VLM agents with progress-weighted SFT, assigning greater weight to steps that advance task progress. Game2Player-9B improves progress from 14.3% to 31.2% on PlayerBench and from 30.0% to 53.1% on the external GameWorld benchmark. More broadly, our work suggests a path for visual agents to scale their gameplay experience by building, verifying, and learning from existing game worlds.

items.abstract: Pretrained Time-Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) provide strong representations for downstream classification tasks. Yet adapting a TSFM under changing operating conditions remains challenging. A model must improve on each newly observed condition without sacrificing conditions it has already learned, often from only a small labeled calibration set and without knowing the operating condition at inference time. We find that this difficulty has an important geometric structure. Under an operating-condition shift, the embedding space of a TSFM does not move uniformly: some local regions change substantially, while others remain nearly unchanged. Consequently, a global adaptation can unnecessarily move embeddings that were already correctly classified. To address this, we propose the novel PACT (Piecewise Adaptation via Chart Transport). PACT partitions the frozen source embedding space into local charts and learns lightweight residual transports for the regions affected by each new condition. An explicit identity path is always retained, and a learned gate softly selects among the identity and accumulated transports for each input. The pretrained TSFM encoder, classifier head, and previously learned transports remain fixed. With only 5% labeled calibration data per arriving condition and no condition identity at test time, PACT maintains an average macro-F1 above 0.95 across a four-condition bearing-fault stream. Under homogeneous tasks and label spaces, similar retention-adaptation behavior is observed across public benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/Sachithx/PACT.

items.abstract: Organizations increasingly deploy downloaded open-weight GUI agents. A backdoored agent passes acceptance tests on clean data and misbehaves only when a visual trigger appears on screen, turning an unvetted checkpoint into a supply-chain risk. However, existing sample-level detectors target image classifiers and CLIP-style encoders, leaving step-level backdoor detection for GUI agents unaddressed. On clean steps, the instruction drives the action; when an unreferenced screen region hijacks the step, the instruction loses control over the decision state or that region dictates it instead. We term this signature intent--evidence dominance inversion and propose IDEA (Intent-Dominance Evidence Audit) to detect backdoor activation at inference time for each step without trigger knowledge or attack data. Specifically, Intent Counterfactual Probing (ICP) measures how far redirected instructions move the decision state, and Region Causal Audit (RCA) quantifies how far ablating a candidate region moves it. A gated conformal score compares both displacements against clean steps at the same distance from the clean manifold, providing a finite-sample false-positive guarantee. Extensive experiments on Qwen2.5-VL-3B across five attack families show that IDEA consistently detects backdoor activation under a controlled false-positive rate and outperforms state-of-the-art detection methods, while localizing the trigger region for every alarm and adding only modest inference overhead.

items.abstract: Abstract Predicting drug-target interactions (DTIs) with deep learning offers opportunities to accelerate drug discovery, yet performance is often constrained by the scarcity of target-specific training data. Transfer learning relieves this limitation but requires choosing a relevant source task, a choice usually made ad hoc. Here we use the Enzyme Commission (EC) classification hierarchy as a systematic criterion for source selection, ascending the EC tree from the target enzyme until a related family carries sufficient ChEMBL bioactivity data to pre-train a deep feedforward network, which is then fine-tuned on the scarce target. We applied this approach to SHMT2 and MTHFD2, two pharmacologically understudied enzymes of the mitochondrial one-carbon (1C) pathway, which is implicated in cancer and fibrosis and supports fibroblast collagen production through glycine synthesis. With 29 active compounds for MTHFD2 and only 6 for SHMT2 which has no ligands of its own, the six coming from its paralogue SHMT1 in the same EC class. EC-guided transfer learning produced usable models in a system where training from scratch failed (Matthews correlation coefficient 0.00 for SHMT2). Virtual screening of the DrugBank library identified six candidates, three of which, carbimazole, crizotinib, and GSK-2018682, reduced TGF-β-induced collagen production and glycine accumulation in human lung fibroblasts. The methodology, datasets, and code are released as a reusable template for enzyme targets with scarce bioactivity coverage.

items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence for science (AI4S) is often discussed as a unified transformation, although scientific domains differ markedly in how model outputs are tested, validated, and justified. We map an audited corpus of N=2,784 records (2014–2025) retrieved from Crossref and screened with a frozen, versioned rulebook, and compare evidence regimes in protein science, materials design, drug discovery, closed-loop experimentation, and mathematical reasoning. Using term co-occurrence, reference co-citation, burst detection, growth models, and collaboration networks, we identify three robust patterns: (i) rapid but decelerating growth (Poisson rate 1.381, 95% CI 1.361–1.402, declining from 1.537 in 2014–2019 to 1.320 in 2019–2025); (ii) a coherent term-co-occurrence structure (75 nodes, modularity Q=0.404 ) organized around four measured streams—representation learning, generative and inverse design, closed-loop experimentation, and neuro-symbolic reasoning—with the generative stream acting as the connecting hub; and (iii) a right-boundary rise in large language model terminology (burst state 3) that a year-by-year backtest shows is not a last-observation artefact. The maps are sensitive to metadata availability: abstract coverage is 50.6%, reference coverage 84.3%, and a title-only variant changes the network partition substantially (adjusted Rand index 0.762), so the maps describe the screened open-metadata corpus rather than the total AI4S literature. Cross-domain analysis shows that AI most consequentially shifts scientific bottlenecks from representation and candidate generation toward experimental or formal validation, provenance, and responsibility for claims. We contribute an auditable, open-metadata science-mapping workflow designed for reproducibility and an evidence-regime framework for analysing how epistemic labour is redistributed across models, instruments, formal verifiers, infrastructures, and human experts.

items.abstract: Introduction The root vole (Microtus oeconomus), a small mammal native to the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, is adapted to chronic high-altitude hypoxia and exhibits a polygynous mating system. whereas the prairie vole (Microtus ochrogaster) from North American grasslands is a model of social monogamy. Oxytocin (OXT) and its receptor (OXTR) play central to prosocial behaviors including pair bonding, yet their sequences and evolutionary implications in the root vole remain unclear. Methods we retrieved cytochrome b, OXT, and OXTR sequences from 21 species via GenBank. Coding and regulatory regions of the OXT and OXTR in the root vole were cloned by PCR, nucleotide and amino acid sequences were aligned using DNAMAN 6 and Multalin tool. Phylogenetic trees were constructed in MEGA X using the neighbor-joining (NJ) method. The three-dimensional (3D) structures of the OXT-OXTR complexes for mouse, M. oeconomus, and M. ochrogaster were predicted with AlphaFold 3. and Hydrogen bonds were analyzed in ChimeraX (1.11.1). Results We cloned the OXT and OXTR coding and regulatory regions from hypothalamus of M. oeconomus. Phylogenetic trees placed M. oeconomus, M. ochrogaster, and Mus musculus in a single major clade, with the two-vole species sharing the same branch. Species-specific sequence variations between the two voles were identified. Predicted 3D structures revealed differences in ligand-receptor binding interfaces and in hydrogen-bond networks across species. Notably, the M. ochrogaster complex contained the greatest number of hydrogen bonds, suggesting a tighter ligand-receptor interaction. Conclusion We propose that variation in the OXT-OXTR hydrogen-bond network, the ligand-binding pocket (TM4), and the intracellular loops IC1 and IC3 may be related to underlie species differences in ligand-receptor binding affinity and, consequently, in pair-bonding behavior.

items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used for de novo small-molecule design, but the practical and translational utility of generated candidates depends on the configuration of the entire discovery workflow rather than on generative model architecture alone. This review adopts a workflow-based perspective on generative molecular design, tracing the process from existing molecular data sets, preprocessing and representation, to molecule generation, conditioning, candidate prioritization, evaluation, and iterative refinement. It examines how generative AI model families, constraints, and predictive oracles interact within this pipeline, and evaluates generated candidates using intrinsic metrics, computational assessments, and experimental and translational evidence. Active learning, computational and experimental feedback, and human expert input are further discussed as mechanisms for closed-loop refinement. Across these stages, we identify data construction and representation choices, oracle quality, evaluation protocols, and the availability of informative feedback as major determinants of how model performance should be interpreted and whether generated structures progress toward biologically and translationally meaningful candidates, with selected examples. In conclusion, reliable generative drug discovery requires coordinated design across the entire workflow rather than isolated advances in individual components.

items.abstract: Background Stanford type A aortic dissection (AAD) is a life-threatening vascular emergency characterized by high mortality and a lack of targeted pharmacological interventions. Cuproptosis, a recently defined copper-dependent regulated cell death modality, has been implicated in various cardiovascular pathologies, yet its specific molecular role in the development of AAD remains largely unexplored. Methods We performed an integrated bioinformatics analysis using three independent GEO datasets (GSE107844, GSE147026, and GSE190635) to identify cuproptosis-related differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in AAD tissues. A panel of diagnostic biomarkers was selected using three machine learning algorithms: Random Forest, Support Vector Machine-Recursive Feature Elimination (SVM-RFE), and Boruta. The expression of identified hub genes was validated in clinical patient samples and a BAPN/Ang II-induced AAD mouse model via qRT-PCR and histological staining. Potential therapeutic agents were identified through the Drug-Gene Interaction Database (DGIdb) and validated using molecular docking. Results A total of 31 cuproptosis-related DEGs were identified. Six key genes were identified via PPI and machine learning algorithms. The differential expression patterns of these genes were validated by qRT-PCR in both AAD mouse model and clinical tissues. Subsequently, clinical correlation analysis revealed that MT1G and NLRP3 expression correlated significantly with inflammatory (white blood cell count, IL-6) and coagulation markers (D-dimer). The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) for MT1G and NLRP3 was comparable to that of D-dimer, indicating their potential value as biomarkers. Via screening using the DGIdb and validation by molecular docking, compounds such as Buthionine sulfoximine (targeting MT1G), dapansutrile (targeting NLRP3), and ARP100 (targeting DBT) demonstrated favorable binding affinity to their targets. Conclusion Our findings suggest that cuproptosis-related genes may play a role in AAD pathogenesis and provide candidate biomarkers and therapeutic leads for further investigation.

items.abstract: Purpose: To develop a data-efficient, clinically guided transfer-learning framework for hyperacute neurological outcome prediction from head CT in patients undergoing extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) after cardiac arrest by leveraging free-text radiology report. Methods: . This retrospective study included 683 patients with available CT examination and radiology reports from December 2015 to November 2025. The primary outcome distinguished favorable neurological outcomes (Cerebral Performance Category [CPC] 1-2) from neurological death due to brain death or cerebral herniation (CPC 5). A cross-attention adaptor jointly learned to predict neurological outcome and five report-derived manifestations of brain injury from a frozen pretrained head CT encoder. Outcome prediction used CT images alone at inference. The manifestation-guided adaptor, trained with and without additional patients who contributed only manifestation labels, was compared with outcome-only adaptor and two pooled-feature baselines. Performance was summarized as mean ± SD across five held-out folds. Results: . Of 683 patients, 197 were eligible for outcome evaluation (63 with favorable outcomes and 134 with neurological death), and 486 formed the manifestation-only cohort. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) was 0.918 ± 0.044 for the outcome-only adaptor. The manifestation-guided adaptor achieved an AUROC of 0.927 ± 0.042. With additional manifestation-only training data, the adaptor achieved the mean AUROC (0.929 ± 0.037), specificity (93.7% ± 6.5%), with a sensitivity of 79.9% ± 9.2%. Conclusion: Manifestation-guided adaptation outperforms outcome-only adaptation for neurological outcome prediction from hyperacute head CT after ECPR. Report-derived manifestation labels enabled training with additional examinations without eligible outcome labels while preserving CT-only prediction.

items.abstract: Background: MRI-guided laser interstitial thermal therapy (LITT) provides minimally invasive option for surgical treatment of recurrent brain tumors. While patient-specific prediction of thermal dose distributions would improve treatment planning, no quantitative methods currently exist for this purpose. Although conventional numerical solvers are being widely investigated, these methods are computationally expensive and often limited by accuracy and reliability. Purpose: Here we propose DeepoLITT, a rapid and accurate model to predict quantitatively heat propagation in LITT procedures. This study represents the first phase of the investigation which focuses on training and validating synthetic datasets to test model , s accuracy, robustness, and computational efficiency. Methods: We built DeepoLITT on a branch–trunk neural network architecture, where the first branch extracts feature from tumor images, the second branch encodes laser parameters (power, duration, and probe orientation), and the trunk models the mapping from spatial coordinates to the resulting temperature field. To train and test the model, we generated synthetic datasets with different noise levels (0~20%) to mimic LITT procedures with two distinct laser probe types (FullFire and SideFire [Monteris, Inc.]) by a FEM (finite element method) solver. The dataset consisted of 400 samples, of which 90% were used for training and validation and 10% for testing. To evaluate spatial similarity of predicted thermal dose distribution against the ground truth, we employed Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) and Hausdorff Distance (HD) computed on CEM43 (Cumulative Equivalent Minutes at 43 °C) isodose contours at thresholds of 2, 10, and 60 minutes. Finally, we evaluated the model , s inference speed with a representative image grid. Results: For the FullFire laser probe, the DeepoLITT model achieved temperature prediction error with average values ranging from 1.16±0.40% to 2.92±0.25%, and peak values ranging from 4.26±1.31% to 14.94±0.43% as data noise increased from 0% to 20%. For the SideFire laser probe, the model achieved temperature prediction error with average values ranging from 3.79±0.53% to 5.13±1.00% and peak values ranging from 15.18±7.15% to 20.75±2.84%. For thermal dose assessment, at the noise-free level for the FullFire laser probe, the model exhibited strong spatial agreement with FEM references, yielding DSCs of 0.96±0.02, 0.97±0.21, and 0.96±0.21 with corresponding HDs of 0.09±0.08 mm, 0.07±0.07 mm, and 0.06±0.08 mm at 2–, 10–, and 60–minute CEM43 thresholds. For the SideFire laser probe, the model achieved DSCs of 0.96±0.02, 0.97±0.21, and 0.96±0.21, with corresponding HDs of 0.20±0.31mm, 0.11±0.30 mm, and 0.15±0.31 mm, respectively. As the noise level increases, these DSC values show a decreasing trend, and the HD values increase. In terms of computational efficiency, the DeepoLITT model inferences temperature maps with 0.04±0.05 seconds per 3D sample ([31 × 31 × 3] grid), compared to 24.32±2.12 seconds required by the FEM solver. Conclusions: The study with synthetic data demonstrates the proposed model is an accurate and rapid method in predicting thermal dose. After testing clinical data, the method has high feasibility to be deployed in real clinical environment.

items.abstract: Cognitive reserve concerns why the same aging causes less decline in some individuals than others, a question that digital twin brains can address by aging each individual in silico. Here we present Brain-VRNN, a connectome-constrained variational recurrent neural network trained on longitudinal multitask functional MRI. Its regenerated brain signals reproduced four functional aging markers of unseen individuals (r = 0.93–0.96) and identified each person (accuracy 0.98). Without cognitive scores, its global latent learned a trait dimension stable within each person, which helped predict future cognition. Crucially, when every individual underwent the same counterfactual aging, those with a lower trait value declined more, yet recovered up to 1.6 times as much with a reduction in body mass index, a modifiable dementia risk factor. Aging single regions showed that different markers decline through different regions, with a lateral temporal–angular region shared by all. Brain-VRNN brings within-person simulation to cognitive reserve.

items.abstract: Abstract Pseudoprogression, transient radiographic worsening caused by treatment-related inflammation rather than tumor growth, is a well-recognized pitfall after chemoradiotherapy for glioblastoma and is becoming more relevant as checkpoint inhibitors and cellular immunotherapies such as chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells enter clinical testing. Conventional structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) cannot reliably separate pseudoprogression from true progression, exposing patients to premature treatment discontinuation or unnecessary intensification. Quantitative, artificial-intelligence-based imaging analysis (radiomics, and its molecular extension radiogenomics) is an emerging candidate solution. In this narrative review we synthesize the evidence on radiomics and radiogenomics for differentiating pseudoprogression from true progression in glioblastoma, with emphasis on the immunotherapy and cellular-therapy context. We summarize the pathobiology and reported frequency of pseudoprogression after standard and immune-based therapies, outline the limitations of current response criteria (RANO, iRANO, RANO 2.0), and review representative studies of texture analysis, hand-crafted radiomics, deep-learning radiomics, and radiogenomics. Although several studies report promising discrimination (reported area-under-the-curve values of approximately 0.88-0.92 in different cohorts), the evidence is limited by small sample sizes, retrospective designs, inconsistent definitions and protocols, and infrequent external validation. Progress will require prospective multicenter cohorts with standardized acquisition and segmentation, adherence to TRIPOD and CLAIM reporting standards, transparent and interpretable models, and integration with clinical, molecular, and liquid-biopsy data. A dedicated evidence base specific to cellular immunotherapy is urgently needed.

items.abstract: Abstract Ring artifacts, caused by detector pixels whose gain or offset is slightly wrong, appear in reconstructed computed tomography (CT) slices as concentric circles around the rotation centre. They can hide small features and break threshold-based segmentation. Classical ring removal relies on hand-tuned filters, and real scans have no ground truth for measuring how well a method works. This project builds a synthetic CT pipeline (phantom, parallel-beam projection, Poisson noise, detector gain and offset error, filtered back-projection) in which the true ring is known for every image, and trains a two-head U-Net that predicts the ring image, which is subtracted from the input, and a ring mask. On 1000 training, 100 validation and 100 test slices of 256 × 256 pixels, where the test slices come from a phantom family never seen in training, the U-Net raises the peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) from 33.11 dB to 39.54 dB and the structural similarity (SSIM) from 0.868 to 0.957. A radial-profile classical baseline tuned on the validation set gains 0.77 dB on validation but loses 0.56 dB on the unseen family. The U-Net gain depends on ring type, from +13.9 dB for dead_hot rings to +0.4 dB for faint band rings. Training with 100, 500 and 1000 images gives 35.29, 38.42 and 39.54 dB; three random seeds give 39.40 ± 0.15 dB; removing the Dice term from the loss raises PSNR to 39.89 dB but lowers mask Dice from 0.640 to 0.605. The mask head is the weaker output (Dice 0.640 overall, 0.07 on band rings). Because all data are simulated, the sim-to-real gap remains the main open question.

items.abstract: Abstract Reliable discrimination between cognitively stable and impaired individuals remains a clinically important challenge in Alzheimer's disease (AD) assessment. Existing multimodal deep learning approaches have predominantly relied on computationally intensive 3D convolutional networks, while relatively few studies jointly model longitudinal imaging and non-imaging data or explicitly account for patient-specific modality contributions. In this work, a multimodal longitudinal framework is proposed that combines 2.5D MRI feature extraction with bidirectional LSTM-based longitudinal sequence encoding. A residual gated fusion mechanism adaptively weights imaging and clinical features for each patient, enabling joint learning of longitudinal and multimodal representations. Structural MRI and clinical data from 204 patients across three longitudinal visits from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) were evaluated using patient-level 5-fold cross-validation to prevent information leakage across visits. The proposed framework achieved a mean AUC of 0.870 ± 0.035, balanced accuracy of 0.802, sensitivity of 0.756, and specificity of 0.847, consistently outperforming unimodal baselines and alternative architectural variants. Ablation studies demonstrated that longitudinal modeling, the 2.5D representation, and residual gated fusion each contributed independently to the overall performance. Quantitative Grad-CAM analysis further revealed cross-visit spatial consistency and significantly greater medial activation in cognitively impaired individuals than in stable individuals, indicating that the model focuses on neuroanatomically plausible regions associated with neurodegenerative change. Our work underscores the potential of multimodal longitudinal deep learning to improve AD assessment while leveraging routinely collected imaging and clinical data.

items.abstract: Abstract Sparse-view computed tomography (CT) reduces radiation dose and scan time by acquiring few projection angles but filtered back-projection (FBP) of such data suffers from severe streak artefacts because the angular sampling falls far below the Nyquist requirement. We study the post-processing approach in which a residual U-Net removes these artefacts from the FBP image, and test it on five synthetic datasets that differ in object class and physics: head phantoms at normal dose, chest phantoms at ten-fold lower dose, aluminium machined parts, photon-starved titanium components, and aluminium resolution targets. Sinograms at 30, 60 and 90 views are simulated with the Beer-Lambert law, Poisson photon statistics and Gaussian read noise, and the network is compared against FBP and the Simultaneous Algebraic Reconstruction Technique (SART), both with settings tuned on validation data. On 150 held-out test images per dataset, the U-Net achieves the highest peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) in all 15 dataset and view settings, improving on the best classical method by 1.9 to 5.8 dB (paired Wilcoxon test, p < 10⁻²⁰ in every setting), and at 30 views it exceeds the PSNR of 180-view FBP on all five datasets, while running in about 20 ms per image on a CPU. Stress tests show the limits of the approach: networks transfer between similar industrial datasets but degrade or harm images of other object classes, fail when the test data are more sparsely sampled or receive ten times fewer photons than in training, and are outperformed by SART on the unseen Shepp-Logan phantom. A network trained on resolution targets does generalise to a resolution plate taken from laboratory data, improving on SART by 2.7 to 3.4 dB. The code, data and trained models are released for full reproducibility.

items.abstract: Abstract Computed Tomography (CT) is a premier non-destructive testing (NDT) modality used for inspecting internal defects, particularly porosity in additive manufacturing and metal castings. The standard industry workflow relies on voxel-wise image segmentation (e.g., Otsu thresholding) to separate void spaces from the solid matrix before calculating the total Porosity Volume Fraction (PVF). However, this segmentation step is highly brittle under severe measurement noise and artifacts, leading to catastrophic miscalculations. In this paper, we propose a direct deep-learning regression approach using a 3D Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) equipped with Global Average Pooling (GAP) to predict scalar PVF directly from noisy 3D CT volumes, bypassing segmentation entirely. To validate this hypothesis, we engineered a rigorous synthetic 3D CT dataset containing 500 procedural phantoms with precisely controlled spherical pores and uniformly distributed PVF ranging from 0.1% to 15%. We degraded these volumes with varying levels of Gaussian noise (10 dB, 20 dB, and 30 dB SNR). The 3D CNN was evaluated against classical Otsu thresholding and a Random Forest (RF) machine learning baseline utilizing global intensity statistics. Our results demonstrate that the 3D CNN is exceptionally robust, maintaining a low Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 0.363 percentage points even under extreme 10 dB noise, where Otsu thresholding catastrophically collapses (MAE of 11.51 pp). Unexpectedly, the RF baseline achieved the lowest overall MAE (0.088 pp). Through a rigorous evidence audit and domain-shift experiment involving a simulated beam-hardening cupping artifact, we dissect this phenomenon, revealing that the RF's superiority is a statistical artifact of the synthetic data's homogenous matrix assumption. This research highlights the viability of segmentation-free volumetric regression for NDT while providing a critical warning regarding 'shortcut learning' in synthetic physics datasets.

items.abstract: Skeletal muscle magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) plays an increasingly important role in the management of neuromuscular diseases, ranging from diagnostic workup to longitudinal follow-up and therapeutic evaluation. Initially based on qualitative radiological image interpretation, it is evolving towards quantitative approaches that provide a sensitive and objective measure of muscle alterations. The fat fraction (FF), obtained notably using Dixon sequences, and water T2 are currently two widely studied biomarkers integrated into numerous clinical trials. FF allows for the characterization and monitoring of fatty replacement, whereas water T2 is a non-specific marker of disease activity, which can normalize with treatment. Advances in deep learning, accelerated multiparametric acquisitions, and whole-body imaging are driving their deployment. However, inter-center standardization, automation, equipment accessibility, and professional training remain major challenges for their integration into clinical routine.

items.abstract: Background Accurate preoperative risk stratification for lymph node metastasis (LNM) in papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) remains difficult. We developed and validated ThyLNT, a Transformer-based 2.5D deep learning model using preoperative computed tomography (CT), and explored related biological features in multi-omics analyses. Methods A total of 1560 patients with PTC from six hospitals were retrospectively included. The Tongji Hospital cohort was divided into training and internal validation sets, and five external cohorts were used for independent testing. Seven 2.5D tumor slices were extracted per patient, encoded with a DenseNet201 backbone, and fused by a Transformer. Model performance was compared with radiomics, ensemble learning, and multi-instance learning using AUC, calibration, decision curve, and precision-recall analyses. Bulk RNA-seq, single-cell RNA-seq, spatial transcriptomics, and spatial metabolomics were used to explore related biological features. Results ThyLNT achieved an AUC of 0.882 (CI, 0.858-0.905) in the training cohort, 0.787 (CI, 0.738-0.835) in the internal validation cohort, and 0.772 (CI, 0.662-0.878) to 0.827 (CI, 0.763-0.885) across the five external cohorts. It showed multicenter discrimination, whereas calibration and threshold-dependent operating characteristics varied across cohorts. Multi-omics analyses provided exploratory biological context, including candidate associations with vascular endothelial growth factor A-related signaling and lipid metabolism. Conclusions ThyLNT demonstrated multicenter performance for preoperative LNM prediction in PTC and may support risk stratification, although calibration, threshold use, and clinical utility require prospective validation.

items.abstract: Background Intracerebral hemorrhage requires rapid mechanism-specific treatment, yet early stroke triage relies on clinical severity scales that do not reliably distinguish hemorrhage from ischemic stroke. We assessed the feasibility of a standardized ultrafast transcranial ultrasound protocol designed to support subsequent artificial intelligence (AI)-based intracerebral hemorrhage detection. Methods HYPER-AI-SCAN (Hyper-Acute AI-Assisted Sonographic Cerebral Hemorrhage Assessment Network) was a single-center prospective feasibility study with embedded exploratory AI analysis. Between March and December 2025, 102 adults with acute computed tomography (CT)-confirmed stroke were prospectively enrolled according to trained operator availability. Primary feasibility outcomes were protocol completion, operator-rated adequate transtemporal windows, and acquisition time. In patients with retrievable paired baseline CT, exploratory AI analyses compared CT-only, ultrasound-only, and cross-modal CT-guided ultrasound models using patient-level area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, sensitivity, and specificity. Results Two patients were excluded after acquisition because insonation depth was <19 cm, yielding 100 evaluable patients (33 intracerebral hemorrhage; 67 ischemic stroke). The protocol was completed in all evaluable patients; adequate transtemporal windows were identified in 87%, and median acquisition time was 22 seconds (interquartile range, 13-31). Paired baseline CT images were available in 91 patients. Mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.86 (SD, 0.07) for the CT-only model, 0.85 (SD, 0.14) for the ultrasound-only model, and 0.92 (SD, 0.07) for the cross-modal model. Conclusions Standardized ultrafast transcranial ultrasound acquisition was feasible at the bedside in acute stroke and generated brief cine-loops suitable for exploratory AI development. Multicenter external validation is required before diagnostic or triage application. Registration information Clinicaltrials.gov. Identifier: NCT07319013.

items.abstract: ObjectiveThe limited interpretability and generalizability of machine learning models for bone mineral density regression hinder their clinical application. This study aimed to develop and evaluate a machine learning model for lumbar bone mineral density regression using computed tomography radiomics and to assess its interpretability through Shapley Additive exPlanations analysis.MethodsIn this retrospective, single-center, cross-sectional study, 150 patients who underwent routine abdominal computed tomography and dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry scans between April 2018 and November 2023 were included. Lumbar vertebral bodies were segmented using 3D-slicer, followed by radiomics feature extraction. Machine learning models, including EXtreme gradient boosting, light gradient boosting machine, gradient boosting decision tree, support vector machine, and random forest, were used for bone mineral density regression and T-score classification. Shapley Additive exPlanations analysis was used to assess global and local interpretability.ResultsThe EXtreme gradient boosting algorithm showed the best performance for bone mineral density regression, with an R 2 of 0.80, mean absolute error of 0.07, mean squared error of 0.01, and Pearson's r of 0.90. The T-score classification achieved a weighted average precision, recall, and F1 score of 0.75, 0.71, and 0.72, respectively. Shapley Additive exPlanations analysis provided global insights into feature contributions and local interpretability for individual samples.ConclusionsThis study introduced an interpretable method using routine computed tomography scans and the EXtreme gradient boosting algorithm to predict lumbar bone mineral density. The top radiomic features identified through Shapley Additive exPlanations analysis, such as Coarseness and RunEntropy, may contribute to accurate bone mineral density prediction.

items.abstract: Objective. Multi-phase coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) provides a clear visualization of coronary arteries, offering comprehensive and reliable imaging support for the clinical diagnosis of coronary artery disease. However, traditional motion correction reconstruction algorithms lack reconstruction robustness despite their interpretability, while deep learning reconstruction methods achieve high imaging quality at the expense of interpretability and anatomical reliability in clinical CCTA practice. This study aims to simultaneously achieve interpretable and robust multi-phase coronary reconstruction. Approach. We propose a motion trajectory estimation and motion correction framework termed sectorized partial-angle reconstruction-based motion correction (SPARC) for CCTA. The proposed framework integrates sectorized partial-angle reconstructions, a spatio-temporal cascaded network for coronary centerline extraction, and a phase-accumulated fuzzy C-means clustering algorithm for motion trajectory estimation. These components work together to minimize motion estimation errors and enhance the quality of motion-corrected reconstruction. Main results . Experimental results from both simulations and clinical studies demonstrate that SPARC achieves superior reconstruction performance compared with existing methods. SPARC effectively reduces coronary motion artifacts and restores clear vessel structures while preserving reconstruction fidelity, achieving the best scores on all metrics. Significance. By preserving both interpretability and anatomical reliability while effectively reducing motion artifacts, SPARC provides a clinically deployable solution for motion-corrected multi-phase CCTA, supporting more reliable imaging for coronary artery disease diagnosis.

items.abstract: Single-cell multi-omics data offer an opportunity to resolve how gene regulatory networks (GRNs) are rewired during cell-fate transitions, but most existing methods infer static snapshots, ignore temporal dependencies or assume linear regulation. Here we present DRAFT, a deep learning framework that combines graph attention with recurrent temporal memory to infer dynamic GRNs from time-resolved single-cell multi-omics data. On simulated data, DRAFT outperforms existing methods in accuracy and temporal smoothness. In mouse cellular reprogramming and Drosophila adult spermatogenesis, it recovers interactions supported by independent ChIP-seq, perturbation and Hi-C data, together with known stage-specific regulators. By inferring regulatory activity from dynamic network structure rather than expression alone, DRAFT identifies regulators whose activity precedes their transcriptional peak, including the candidate early germline regulator Mondo. Germline-specific Mondo knockdown alters germline stem cell number and expression of the predicted targets kuz and mamo. DRAFT also enables nonlinear alignment of co-developing lineages and reveals stage-specific cell-cell communication.

items.abstract: Spatial omics has generated measurements at unprecedented scale, yet computational approaches remain largely confined to individual modalities and 2D representations. Here we assemble ImageOmicsNet-300M, a corpus of 300 million single-cell and spatial transcriptomic profiles, including 24.9 million H&E-predicted virtual spatial transcriptomics profiles, and 4,623 H&E sections. Of these H&E sections, we generated 1,782 from aging mouse organs and serially sectioned human skin spanning five decades, with matched spatial transcriptomics and snRNA-seq. Building on this resource, we develop GenVinci, a multimodal tissue foundation model that reconstructs 3D tissue scenes from routine 2D histology. GenVinci predicts spatial gene expression from H&E with zero-shot generalization and maps senescence-associated states across 85.8 million cells, revealing cell-type-specific patterns and disease-associated remodeling. Integration with human genetics implicates suprabasal keratinocytes in atopic dermatitis and keratinocyte carcinomas, linked to higher and lower p16 and p21 expression, respectively. These findings establish GenVinci as a framework mapping senescence in 3D across scales.

items.abstract: Subcellular-resolution spatial transcriptomics localizes individual RNA transcripts within cells with high-precision. Existing methods for identifying spatially organized cell populations rely on cellular niches defined by neighboring cells, leaving open whether such populations can be identified from individual-cell representations alone. Moreover, representations that jointly capture transcript identity and three-dimensional (3D) spatial organization have not been systematically learned or biologically evaluated. Here we present a representation learning framework that models each cell as a gene-annotated point cloud of transcripts and trains a rotation-equivariant neural network to reconstruct 3D cell shape, yielding spatially informed transcript embeddings. We further aggregate these embeddings into a cell-state representation that summarizes transcript-level spatial patterns. Our framework outperforms existing point-cloud-based 3D reconstruction methods on cell-shape reconstruction. In MERFISH human uterine cancer, combining the learned embeddings with gene expression improved prediction of CD45RO protein intensity over both gene expression alone and niche-based embeddings. Applied to MERFISH human liver cancer and Xenium human lung datasets, our framework identified distinct spatial patterns between cell populations, including spatially organized subpopulations marked by disease-associated gene expression and patterns associated with pathological tissue structures. Together, these results show that learning transcript representations through 3D cell reconstruction provides a novel approach to capture cell-state heterogeneity and biologically relevant spatial organization in subcellular spatial transcriptomics.

items.abstract: Cells suppress protein synthesis during starvation, but how translation recovers upon nutrient repletion remains poorly understood. To address this gap, we followed translational recovery in budding yeast after repletion of glucose, nitrogen, or phosphate, combining time-resolved metabolomics, structural proteomics, transcriptomics, and spike-in-calibrated ribosome profiling. Nutrient addition rapidly altered ribosome occupancy in distinct, transcript-specific programs. To identify their sequence determinants, we developed RiboNet, a deep learning framework that predicts ribosome load and positions along transcripts from mRNA sequence. RiboNet-guided in silico mutagenesis revealed reduced pausing at serine codons upon glucose repletion and transiently increased pausing at leucine codons following nitrogen repletion. These responses coincided with altered cognate tRNA charging and metabolite-associated structural changes in aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases. RiboNet also identified a conserved 5′ UTR motif, GAUY, that increased reporter protein output following glucose repletion. Our findings reveal how metabolic state alters the contributions of mRNA sequence features to translation initiation and elongation.

items.abstract: Abstract Background Late-life depression (LLD) is associated with an increased risk of dementia and a biologically defined subgroup exhibits amyloid pathology associated with Alzheimer’s disease (AD). However, the molecular and neuroanatomical characteristics of this subgroup remain incompletely understood. Investigating the relationships among plasma proteomic profiles, T1-derived radiomic features, and cognition may help characterize biological heterogeneity at the intersection of LLD and the AD continuum. Methods This integrative proteomics–radiomics study included 116 LLD patients, whose AD biomarker status was defined using Core 1 biomarkers according to the 2024 Alzheimer’s Association revised criteria. A machine learning–derived radiomic signature distinguishing biomarker-defined amyloid-positive from amyloid-negative LLD was constructed. The key plasma proteomic module was identified using weighted gene co-expression network analysis, and its mechanistic role was evaluated using mediation analysis. Results The radiomic score (RadScore) discriminated biomarker-defined amyloid-positive LLD in a held-out internal test subset (AUC = 0.788), with influential features from the paracentral lobule and precuneus. It correlated with a neutrophil activation–enriched module (r = − 0.49, p < 0.001). The cross-sectional indirect-effect analysis indicated that the RadScore accounted for 52.5% of the modeled association with memory performance. Conclusions In biomarker-defined amyloid-positive LLD, T1-derived radiomic features were associated with a plasma protein module enriched for innate immune and neutrophil-related annotations and with memory performance. These cross-modal associations require independent longitudinal validation.

items.abstract: Despite major advances in plant genomics, researchers' ability to predict complex trait variation remains limited by an incomplete understanding of the regulatory genome. Cis-regulatory elements (CREs) and their organisation into cis-regulatory modules (CRMs) form the building blocks of the regulatory grammar, yet their variability at the intra- and interspecific levels, context dependence, and poor annotation have long hindered their systematic use in plant science. We review how recent progress in deep learning and integrative modelling marks a turning point for deciphering plant regulatory grammar. Moving beyond sequence-centric motif discovery, we highlight the need for plant-oriented, context-aware, and evolution-informed frameworks that explicitly learn and interpret the regulatory grammar. Integrating CRE and CRM predictions into gene regulatory networks, knowledge graphs, and genomic prediction models will be pivotal to bridging regulatory sequences, phenotypes, and environments. Beyond fundamental insight, understanding the cis-regulatory code opens new avenues for causal variant prioritisation, regulatory engineering, and ultimately regulation-aware precision breeding and agronomic decision-making. Deciphering plant regulatory grammar is therefore both a scientific and a societal priority, with the potential to maximise breeding efficiency and support the development of fine-tuned agronomic management practices.

items.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) requires robust biomarkers and therapeutic targets. This study aimed to identify secretome-associated genes with diagnostic, prognostic, and tumor-suppressive relevance in CRC, focusing on GUCA2B (uroguanylin). We integrated single-cell transcriptomics, pseudobulk differential expression, machine learning (ML), multi-omics, and in vitro functional assays (HCT-116 cells). ML consensus feature selection across four algorithms identified 20 shared features from 850 downregulated genes; eight genes, including GUCA2B, were selected by all four models, forming the finalized signature. GUCA2B was markedly reduced in CRC epithelium. A frozen eight-gene logistic model showed an apparent (training-set) AUC of 0.998 in TCGA-COADREAD and maintained discrimination in three independent cohorts (AUC = 0.881-0.974). Reduced GUCA2B expression correlated with adverse survival, promoter hypermethylation, and altered immune infiltration. In vitro, GUCA2B restoration induced intrinsic apoptosis (increased BAX, decreased BCL2), reduced viability, and impaired migration; because GC-C/cGMP dependence was not tested, these effects constitute receptor-mechanism-agnostic proof of concept. In conclusion, GUCA2B represents a candidate epithelial-restricted CRC biomarker and tumor-suppressive gene. While the frozen multi-gene model shows promise for diagnostic stratification and GUCA2B restoration demonstrates preliminary tumor-suppressive activity, the small discovery set (n = 23 pseudobulk samples), moderate feature-selection stability, and single-cell-line validation necessitate cautious interpretation. Prospective clinical validation and in vivo multi-model studies are required before diagnostic or therapeutic application.

items.abstract: Regression analysis of high-throughput omics data is often made difficult by noise, batch effects, and the loss of information resulting from the discretization of continuous variables. Existing machine learning algorithms often struggle to extract stable biological signals under these heterogeneous conditions. We introduce BI-SCUDO Regression, a rank-based regression framework designed for omics data analysis. By leveraging within-sample rankings and network-based predictions, BI-SCUDO Regression bypasses the need for complex normalization and provides robust, interpretable results. In synthetic benchmarks, BI-SCUDO Regression demonstrated strong resilience to noise, maintaining predictive and feature-selection stability under conditions in which standard models exhibited performance degradation. When applied to cohorts from TCGA datasets, BI-SCUDO Regression consistently outperformed LASSO, Random Forest Regression, and XGBoost in predicting survival, with an average increase in Ratio of Performance to Deviation ranging from 43% to 86%, depending on the comparator. Furthermore, the algorithm consistently identified parsimonious, statistically significant, and biologically relevant biomarkers, with enrichment for cancer-related terms across all stage stratifications. Although BI-SCUDO Regression incurs higher training times due to its genetic optimization strategy, it offers a robust and interpretable approach to outcome prediction and biomarker discovery, with potential applications in precision medicine, where noisy data compromise the performance of conventional regression methods.

items.abstract: Importance: Consumers use conversational artificial intelligence (AI) for health at scale, but whether purpose-built medical AI is used primarily for information seeking or as an entry point into care remains unclear. Objective: To characterize the clinical concepts users present, their visit intentions, and progression to physician telehealth care in real-world consultations on a purpose-built medical AI platform. Design: Exploratory retrospective cohort study of consultations sampled in equal monthly numbers between June 1, 2025, and June 30, 2026. Setting: A free, publicly available, consumer-facing, anonymous-by-default medical AI platform. Participants: Random sample of 26,000 English-language consultations by users aged 18 years or older, each with at least 5 chat interaction rounds. Exposure: A chat consultation with the medical AI. Main Outcomes and Measures: Clinical concepts linked approximately to SNOMED CT; visit intentions classified with a prespecified 11-category schema and reclassified with a published 12-category consumer-health taxonomy; completion of the AI consult with a structured SOAP note; and progression to a completed physician telehealth visit. Automated extraction pipelines were validated against physician annotation in a random subsample. Results: Of 26,000 sampled consultations, 56.7% were by users recorded as female and 50.9% by users aged 18 to 34 years. Among 25,975 consultations with successful extraction, 77,597 clinical concepts were identified; headache, abdominal pain, fatigue, and fever were the most common presenting concepts. Of 55,257 classified intentions, 60.1% (95% CI, 59.7%-60.5%) concerned a new or worsening condition. When consultations were reclassified with the published consumer-health taxonomy, 74.3% (95% CI, 73.8%-74.8%) included symptom questions or health concerns, whereas 5.0% (95% CI, 4.7%-5.2%) included health information or education, reversing the rank order published for a general-purpose assistant. Overall, 53.9% of sampled consultations ended with a structured SOAP note, and 15.1% of those progressed to a completed physician telehealth review. Conclusions and Relevance: Users of this purpose-built medical AI platform predominantly presented active personal health problems rather than general information requests. Symptom-driven use, generation of structured clinical documentation, and progression to physician care suggest that purpose-built medical AI may function as an entry point to clinical care for some users.

items.abstract: Accurate identification of immunogenic neoantigens is critical for personalized cancer vaccines but remains hindered by the high false-positive rates of current predictors. Here, we present DeepOmicsNeo, a modular deep learning framework that harmonizes three biological determinants of immunogenicity. The first module, DeepOmicsNeo-Binding, overcomes data scarcity in non-9mer peptide-Class I Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) binding prediction via a novel augmentation strategy that synthesizes pseudo-binders and non-binders by editing non-anchor residues, outperforming its competitors. The second module, DeepOmicsNeo-Selfness, addresses the paucity of negative training data for immunogenicity prediction by utilizing a Generative Adversarial Network trained on around 60 million human self-peptides. This unsupervised approach quantifies selfness to detect immunogenic peptides and the resulting score correlated with IFN-γ secretion by T-cells. The third module, DeepOmicsNeo-H2, exploits the central-region homology between known HLA Class-I and Class-II restricted epitopes. The integrated model, DeepOmicsNeo-Immunogenicity, outperforms state-of-the-art predictors on the TESLA, HiTIDE, and TiTANIAN benchmark datasets.[세오2.1] Top20 precision, the most important benchmark for clinical utility in personalized cancer vaccine design, was drastically improved over other predictors. Together, these findings indicate that jointly modeling the three complementary features captures biologically meaningful determinants of immunogenicity, supporting DeepOmicsNeo as a robust computational framework for neoantigen prioritization in personalized cancer immunotherapy.

items.abstract: Pathogenic variation across the TP63-IRF6-GRHL3 transcriptional network causes syndromic and nonsyndromic orofacial clefts (OFCs), yet scalar sequence predictors collapse distinct failure modes and leave isoform-specific coding variants, splice-altering indels, and distal enhancer alleles unresolved. Here, we integrate 29 AlphaFold 3 (AF3) assemblies (10 wild-type, 19 mutant), thermodynamic stability (ΔΔG) calculations, and AlphaGenome regulatory modeling across clinical, saturation-mutagenesis, and reporter benchmarks. In strict leave-one-gene-out (LOGO) coding benchmarks, replacing paralog crystal templates with full-length human AF3 structures improves IRF6 classification (biophysical AUROC rising from 0.7844 to 0.8967; ΔΔG from 0.6461 to 0.8516) and resolves canonical isoform gaps in the 602-residue MANE Select GRHL3 homodimer. Projecting IRF6 missense variants onto a two-dimensional stability-versus-interface phase plane separates dominant-negative popliteal pterygium syndrome (PPS) poisons from haploinsufficient Van der Woude syndrome (VWS1) alleles (VWS1-versus-PPS Quadrant I odds ratio [OR] = 0.0263 [reciprocal OR = 38.0], p = 4.652 × 10 -3 ) and distinguishes DNA-contact poisons from dimer-unfolding alleles across 12 zebrafish in vivo assays. Atomistic base-readout contacts in the AF3 TP63-MCS9.7 tetramer mirror loss-of-function profiles in MaveDB (ρ = 0.6048, p = 6.52 × 10 -4 ) and AlphaGenome keratinocyte DNase predictions (ρ = 0.6040, p = 6.65 × 10 -4 ). Across non-coding benchmarks, AlphaGenome splicing tracks reach an AUROC of 0.9876 while prioritizing cryptic splice variants of uncertain significance, and epithelial chromatin tracks capture enhancer grammar, plasmid-cloning artifacts, and context-dependent ARHGAP29, FOXE1, and local 8q24 chromatin effects within AlphaGenome's 1.049-Mb horizon.

items.abstract: This study investigated whether eye-tracking responses to expectancy violations and self-referential processing can objectively classify depression diagnosis and risk. Fifty participants (15 with Major Depressive Disorder, 35 healthy controls) viewed vignettes ending with a final critical word that was either congruent with a positive or negative outcome while eye movements were recorded at a sampling rate of 1000 Hz. Vignettes were presented in either third-person non-self-referential or first-person self-referential formats. All participants completed depression assessments using the Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II) and Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9). Nineteen eye-tracking features were extracted from epochs, time-locked to critical word onset, including saccade dynamics, fixation patterns, pupil responses, and gaze entropy. Random Forest classifiers were trained using a 60-40 train-test split and 20-fold cross validation to predict clinical diagnosis, BDI risk, and PHQ-9 risk categories. Saccade-related measures consistently differentiated between groups, while pupil dilation responses indicated expectancy violation processing. Machine learning classification achieved 83.8% accuracy for clinical diagnosis, 81.0% for BDI risk, and 71.2% for PHQ-9 risk. Self-referential stimuli contributed more heavily to successful classification than non-self-referential stimuli, with saccade displacement and velocity measures being the most important features. Several eye-tracking features, including saccades, pupil dilation, and entropy impacted model performance. These findings demonstrate that eye-tracking responses to semantic expectancy violations can provide objective biomarkers for depression classification, potentially offering a valuable tool for clinical assessment when traditional self-report measures may be unreliable or unavailable.

items.abstract: Abstract Background Early risk stratification after intensive care unit (ICU) admission may inform treatment intensity, goals-of-care discussions, and resource allocation. Developing and maintaining supervised machine learning models requires large labelled cohorts and technical infrastructure that may not be available in all settings. General-purpose large language models (LLMs) can generate risk estimates with human-readable rationales, but their performance and reasoning quality across independent healthcare systems remain uncertain. Methods We analysed three ICU cohorts: eICU-CRD (208 US hospitals), MIMIC-IV (US), and a Korean tertiary-hospital subset of K-MIMIC (Korea). Seven-day mortality after ICU admission was predicted from routinely collected demographic, laboratory, and vital sign variables recorded during the first 24 hours. Six supervised machine learning and deep learning models were developed in eICU-CRD and externally validated in MIMIC-IV and K-MIMIC. GPT-5 and Gemini-2.5-Pro were evaluated with four prompting strategies in 2,000-stay samples per cohort, without cohort-specific training or task-specific fine-tuning. Clinical concepts mentioned in GPT-5 rationales were compared with patient-level predictor importance from an XGBoost reference model; two clinicians rated 150 rationales for clinical trustworthiness. Results Analyses included 124,020, 84,926, and 6,673 ICU stays. Among supervised models, the highest area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) was 0.936 for XGBoost in the held-out eICU-CRD set, 0.858 for the multilayer perceptron in MIMIC-IV, and 0.957 for XGBoost in K-MIMIC. In the corresponding 2,000-stay LLM evaluation samples, GPT-5 achieved AUROCs of 0.925, 0.822, and 0.926, respectively, but generally had a lower area under the precision–recall curve (AUPRC) and, at evaluated operating thresholds, lower specificity. Overlap with the five most influential concepts was partial (precision, 0.47; recall, 0.55), but mentioned concepts had greater mean patient-level importance than nonmentioned concepts in 98.1% of patients (P < 0.001). Clinician-rated trustworthiness averaged 4.03 ± 0.63 on a 5-point scale, with ratings within one point in 83% of cases. Conclusions Supervised models generally achieved the highest discrimination for 7-day mortality after ICU admission. GPT-5 achieved high discrimination without cohort-specific training or task-specific fine-tuning, and its patient-specific rationales preferentially referenced influential predictors and received favorable clinician ratings. Prospective evaluation of reasoning faithfulness and clinical utility is required before clinical use.

items.abstract: Abstract Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in medical training, but evidence from African residency programs is scarce. We assessed how internal medicine residents in Ethiopia use GenAI and how they perceive its impact on clinical learning and clinical decision-making. Methods We conducted an explanatory sequential mixed-methods study consisting of a national cross-sectional online survey of internal medicine residents (June to August 2026), followed by two focus group discussions (FGDs) with 10 residents at two universities (September 2026) to explain the survey findings. Perceived impact was measured with five-point Likert items and two composite scores (learning, five items; decision-making, eight items). Associations with frequency of use were tested with chi-square or Fisher's exact tests. FGD data were organized deductively into categories based on the survey topics. Results Of 252 respondents from 18 institutions, 98.8% had used GenAI and 75.4% used it daily; ChatGPT was used by 91.6% of users. The mean composite score for perceived impact on clinical learning was 3.83 out of 5 (70.7% high) and for clinical decision-making 3.86 out of 5 (67.7% high). Agreement was highest for improved differential diagnosis (90.8%), learning efficiency (81.9%) and support for self-directed learning (79.5%), and lowest for ward-round performance (64.3%) and confidence in complex cases (71.4%). Daily use was more frequent among residents with more than three hours of daily internet use (82.3% versus 66.7% to 67.4%; p = 0.024) and was not associated with age, sex, marital status, year of residency, device access or formal training. In the FGDs, residents described GenAI as a fast, supportive tool for learning and clinical work, as an aid to reasoning and not a replacement for physician judgment, and as a possible threat to independent learning. Conclusions Residents perceive GenAI as helpful for self-directed learning and diagnostic reasoning while keeping final responsibility for clinical decisions. These findings reflect perceptions and not measured outcomes, so objective evaluation of its effects on learning and clinical performance is needed.

items.abstract: Abstract Glucagon-like receptor agonists and incretin-based therapies improve glycaemic control and weight-related outcomes, but individual treatment responses vary. This review examines treatment-response prediction and the clinical evidence relevant to personalised treatment selection. The current evidence table contains 44 records identified through searches in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science. These records comprise a mixture of prediction and predictor analyses, clinical efficacy studies, and other evidence of response to treatment; they should not be interpreted as 44 independently validated AI prediction systems. The synthesis describes therapeutic targets, data sources, and analytical approaches. However, incomplete study-level extraction and unresolved classification issues prevent reliable estimates of prediction-model validation practices, explainability uptake, or comparative algorithm performance. We also propose the Artificial Intelligence Translational Readiness Framework (AI-TRF), comprising external validation, explainability, temporal modelling, prospective evaluation, and clinical implementation. AI-TRF has not been applied to individual studies or empirically validated. Reproducible searches, verified study-level extraction, and independent evaluation remain necessary to establish the clinical readiness of treatment-response prediction systems in this field.

items.abstract: Abstract Background. Ambient clinical AI — software that listens to a consultation and drafts the clinical note, often called an AI scribe — is now a flagship use of artificial intelligence in healthcare. Most tools delivering it are proprietary and cloud-based: consultation audio leaves the building, errors cannot be independently characterised, and the clinician who signs the note answers for output nobody outside the vendor can examine. Open, fully local alternatives that a clinician or researcher can inspect, run and modify remain rare. Objective. This paper reports OpenConsult, an open-source AI scribe with live clinical decision support that runs entirely on one machine in the consulting room and is inspectable end to end, and describes its formative evaluation. Methods. Evaluation was formative and used synthetic consultations only (scripted and acted). Automated tests ran fifteen scripted consultations with pre-written marking schemes, checking transcription quality gates, the urgency alarm’s behaviour across emergency and routine scripts, and whether every cited claim in a note points to a real transcript line. Five acted consultations followed in a real consulting room, and the AI assistants that built the system ran an adversarial security audit under the developer’s direction. The work is reported against the applicable DECIDE-AI items, one stage before live clinical evaluation. Results. OpenConsult is a fully local, open-source consultation assistant, built by a practising general practitioner directing AI coding assistants, running on a single consumer graphics card. It transcribes the consultation live and separates the speakers, drafts a structured clinical note with every sentence linked to its supporting transcript words, runs live decision support whose urgency alarm is shown only to the doctor, drafts referral letters, and offers a supervised spoken history-taking mode. In generated notes, 301 of 302 citations pointed to real transcript lines — an existence check, with clinical faithfulness unmeasured pending independent rating; the one uncited claim was flagged for manual checking. The urgency alarm fired in all eight scripted emergencies and stayed silent in six of seven routine consultations. Five acted consultations surfaced five defects the automated checks had missed, four of them serious; all were fixed, each pinned by a regression test. The security audit returned twelve findings, including one critical vulnerability, fixed and verified before any public exposure. Conclusions. OpenConsult is a working, auditable proof of concept — not yet a validated clinical tool — released for research and education only, with real patient care out of scope. It is intended as an open research instrument: it records whether the reviewing clinician opened the cited evidence before approving, how long review takes, and every revision of its decision support, making human review of ambient clinical AI measurable. Independent, prospective evaluation is required before any step toward care.

items.abstract: Structure-based machine learning is widely expected to advance antibody engineering, yet it is unclear how far affinity predictions transfer to new targets, and why. We introduce a noise-corrected, censoring-aware estimator of the cross-target transfer ceiling, ρ max = √(T/(T+I)), which separates a transferable antibody-intrinsic component (T) from a non-transferable target-specific interaction (I). On deterministic synthetic ground truth the estimator recovers the noise-free ceiling to ± 0.0003, whereas the naive sum-of-squares estimator is biased downward by measurement noise. Applying it from synthetic to real systems, the transferable budget is small, and on real neutralization panels it is not an artefact: the target-specific interaction survives noise and censoring correction. It is strongly regime-dependent, with a two-tier structure: predicting a novel antibody from sequence alone (the design setting) reaches a lower ceiling (ρ ≈ 0.44 on real breadth data) than ranking a characterized one (ρ ≈ 0.59), even with a strong protein language model. Synthetic oracles also overstate transferability: an oracle scored on real predicted structures carries about half the budget of a matched synthetic lattice (0.45 vs. 0.81), and real neutralization and escape panels sit well below the synthetic ceiling (0.32-0.68). Under leakage-free antigen-cluster splits, cross-target affinity ranking across every method family collapses to this budget, while within a sampled target a structure-based graph network ranks affinity above off-the-shelf FoldX and GearBind (within-complex Spearman 0.55), and structural surface descriptors predict a surface-driven developability property (hydrophobic aggregation) where sequence-dominated properties (humanness, charge-driven self-association) do not benefit. A controlled ablation attributes the residual within-target signal to the antibody alone: dropping the antigen from the structural model leaves it essentially unchanged (interface Δ ρ between -0.01 and +0.02 across four panels), so for this model the paratope-epitope interface adds no ranking signal over the antibody alone. Models climb toward the budget within a target — via a measure-then-rank operating mode that recovers top binders 6-8 times more efficiently than random once a target has been sampled — but none crosses it.

items.abstract: Small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) is routinely used for the structural characterization of protein monomers in solution, and computational prediction methods such as AlphaFold now provide accurate atomic models for most proteins. When a predicted model and the experimental scattering curve disagree, several refinement strategies exist, but selecting the appropriate one remains difficult, particularly for users without SAXS modeling expertise. ATSASfold is a web server developed to help analyse the results of SAXS measurements on protein monomers and select appropriate refinement strategies. From a provided experimental SAXS curve, ATSASfold performs primary data analysis, gives a general assessment of macromolecules shape, size, possible aggregation state and data quality. An AlphaFold-generated model is fitted against the SAXS curve and the agreement with the experiment is evaluated. In cases where the fit shows significant discrepancies, a machine-learning classifier trained on SASBDB depositions assigns the case to one of four categories, suggesting the most relevant ATSAS-based strategy for model refinement: fixed model fitting, rigid-body modelling, normal-mode analysis or ensemble optimization. When needed, a graphical interface allows the user to adjust domains or flexible regions of the protein before submitting the structure to ATSAS online for longer fitting jobs. After the fitting is completed, ATSASfold provides a summary of the results. The workflow was tested on examples from the SASBDB open web-databank. These use cases demonstrate smooth operation of the web server and show how ATSASfold can simplify the transition from SAXS data collection to structure-based interpretation.

items.abstract: Video world models keep the world in the context of a generator, so a revisit is synthesized again and earlier edits can drift or disappear. We present WM^MLLM, the first interactive world model built on multimodal large language models (MLLMs), for persistent, editable world generation from a single image. WM^MLLM keeps the world state outside every generator, as a panorama with a revision history, and lets the MLLMs write it: they turn each request into operations on this state, select where a local edit is written, and check every candidate before it becomes the next state. Image generators only propose views, and video only presents them. Users can walk to new places and return, edit objects through text or a box, place subjects, and change lighting, weather or season. By construction, a revisit at the same revision reproduces the earlier view exactly, a local edit leaves every panorama pixel outside its region unchanged, and each request starts from the result of the previous one. Against six world model baselines on MBench-A, WM^MLLM has the highest mean on all four environment-recovery metrics (Epipolar 91.5 versus 0.1 to 74.0) and completes the most camera round trips (85.3% versus at most 50.9%). It has the best value in all 15 CompBench columns against 15 baselines. On 112 local edits judged blind, selecting the region to write after generation raises completion from 34.8% to 83.0%. On 258 WBench and MBench-A items, all 46 revisits recover their earlier views, and all 97 local edits that pass the check leave panorama pixels outside their region unchanged.

items.abstract: Arm-free quadrupeds can perform loco-manipulation, walking on three legs while manipulating with a front leg, yet no existing policy for it follows language instructions. World action models (WAMs) have emerged as effective language-conditioned manipulation policies, but are pretrained for robot arms and sample slowly. WAM-Policy turns one WAM into a quadrupedal loco-manipulation policy via two stages. The first, Cross-Morphology Policy Adaptation and Acceleration, adapts the arm-centric WAM to quadrupeds and distills the transferred policy into a student with one video and two action steps by on-policy self-distillation (OPSD). This student, however, is bounded by its teacher, which only imitates demonstrations. The second stage, Task-Specific Improvement and Merging, therefore tunes the teacher by reinforcement learning (RL) and merges the slow specialists into one few-step student by multi-teacher on-policy distillation (M-OPD). On QLM-Bench, ten simulated tasks with 1,000 demonstrations synthesized without teleoperation, the transferred policy reaches 77.0%, and the OPSD student keeps 76.7% while sampling 14 times faster. Task-specific RL and M-OPD lift it to 85.0%. We also deploy the OPSD student on a real Unitree Go2 Air. WAM-Policy thus achieves a stronger quadrupedal policy at a fraction of the inference cost.

items.abstract: Hybrid attention models combine full and linear attention to achieve a better quality--efficiency trade-off. Converting pretrained Transformers into such models requires identifying which layers should retain full attention under a prescribed budget. We identify two off-policy mismatches in FlashMorph's layer selection: (i) continuous branch interpolation and teacher-forced hidden states differ from discrete hybrid computation; and (ii) frozen model weights fail to account for parameter adaptation during subsequent recovery. We introduce FlashMorph2, an on-policy layer-selection method that (I) evaluates sampled discrete hybrid architectures end to end using their own hidden states, and (II) jointly optimizes layer-selection scores and model weights under the recovery objective to reflect post-adaptation performance. Experiments across Qwen3 model scales and linear-attention variants show that FlashMorph2 consistently outperforms existing layer-selection methods, improving average scores over FlashMorph by +2.42 points on RULER, +1.08 on LongBench, and +0.76 on recall-intensive tasks, while completing layer selection in only 0.72--3.57 GPU hours across 0.6B--8B models, demonstrating high efficiency and scalability.
