items.abstract: Abstract Background: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into clinical decision-making creates uncertainty regarding responsibility and accountability when adverse outcomes occur. Despite this, data regarding stakeholder perspectives remain scarce, especially quantitative data comparing physician and public views on responsibility allocation and transparency. This study aims to evaluate and compare how physicians and the general population in Sweden attribute responsibility for negative medical outcomes when AI is used to support healthcare decisions in primary care, as well as their views on the necessity of transparently disclosing AI use to patients. Methods: A nationwide, cross-sectional, mixed-methods survey was conducted in Sweden between February and May 2025. The survey targeted two distinct cohorts (N = 500 per group): licensed physicians under 70 years, sampled from the National Board of Health and Welfare register, and adults aged 18 or older sampled from the Swedish population registry. The survey used case vignettes as background for multiple-choice questions, with complementary open-ended free-text responses. The data was evaluated using comparative statistical analysis and reflexive thematic analysis. Results: Physicians were significantly more likely than the general population to assign responsibility to the physician (92\% vs. 74\%) and to favor a shared responsibility model involving the physician (48\% vs. 35\%). In contrast, the general population more frequently selected non-physician actor combinations (26\% vs. 8\%) and assigned greater responsibility to the patient in a scenario involving direct patient-AI interaction without a physician involved. Neither group broadly assigned responsibility to the AI itself (1.3\% physicians vs. 10\% general population). The reflexive thematic analysis reinforced these results, identifying a shared accountability framework where all actors share responsibility, but where the physician serves as the ultimate safeguard. A majority of the general population (68\%) affirmed the patient's right to always know if AI was used, in contrast to only 23\% of physicians who exhibited a polarised distribution. Conclusion: Respondents endorse a shared responsibility model among actors involved in implementing and using AI for medical decisions. The physician is viewed as the essential human-in-the-loop, bearing ultimate accountability for adverse outcomes of AI-assisted medical decisions according to a vast majority of respondents. Divergent perspectives regarding transparency emphasise the need to clarify informed consent standards for AI deployment in healthcare.

items.abstract: Abstract Background Small-cell lung cancer (SCLC) is aggressive and often metastatic at diagnosis, and skeletal-related events such as bone pain, pathological fracture and spinal cord compression alter treatment decisions. Prediction tools for bone metastasis in elderly patients with SCLC remain scarce, and external validation and interpretability analyses are limited. We therefore developed and externally validated an interpretable machine learning model for bone metastasis at initial diagnosis in these patients, using routinely available clinical and staging information. Methods We retrospectively enrolled 1,387 consecutive patients aged ≥ 60 years with SCLC treated at two hospitals (2010–2024), randomly divided 7:3 into training and internal validation sets. Two external cohorts were assembled: 128 patients from another hospital (2010–2024) and 19,561 patients from the SEER database (2010–2015). The outcome was bone metastasis at initial diagnosis. Boruta selected features from 16 candidate variables. Six models—logistic regression, decision tree, random forest, XGBoost, LightGBM and artificial neural network—were compared for discrimination and calibration, with decision curve analysis and SHAP interpretation. Results Boruta confirmed four features: N stage, SCLC stage (limited-stage or extensive-stage), liver metastasis and clinical stage. LightGBM was the most stable across cohorts. SHAP identified clinical stage as the largest contributor, with extensive-stage disease, concurrent liver metastasis and higher N stage increasing the predicted risk. Conclusions A LightGBM model based on four features available at initial diagnosis provides stable, interpretable risk stratification for bone metastasis in elderly patients with SCLC and may support clinical decision-making, although recalibration should precede use in other populations.

items.abstract: Abstract Background: Differentiating between bipolar disorder (BD) and borderline personality disorder (BPD) is an intriguing clinical challenge that has attracted research attention, as the multiple co-occurring symptoms such as mood instability, impulsivity, and emotional dysregulation have made the boundary between the two disorders unclear. Recent research in computational psychiatry has shown promise in leveraging the power of knowledge graphs and large language models to enable accurate and inter­pretable decision-making. Methods: The study developed a hybrid framework, KG-Psy, that combines large language models with dynamic graphs. The system extracts clinical entities through GPT-5 while employing multi-step reasoning to find hidden connections within a psychiatric knowledge graph that weighs its evidence-based content. The system performs four main operations, which include extracting clinical entities, creating dynamic weighted knowledge graphs, using GPT-5 to trace multi-step cognitive pathways, and evaluating customized treatment options. The researchers used 310 anonymized psychiatric case re­ports to test their method. Results: KG-Psy achieved better discrimination between BD and BPD than other methods. The model achieved a maximum Precision (%) of 91.5, an improvement of 19%, 10.3%, and 7.4% over the KG-only, LLM-only, and Hybrid-other approaches, respectively. The system successfully discovered un­known cognitive pathways, which it used to create accurate pathway maps and provide treatment rec­ommendations supported by numerical evidence. The results of ablation experiments showed that LLM reasoning, combined with the knowledge graph structure, led to high performance. Conclusion: The KG-Psy system introduces a novel approach to psychiatry inspired by large-scale language models and dynamic graphs that integrates data-driven linguistic analysis with established symbolic knowledge to enhance the capabilities of differential diagnosis and treatment development for complex mood and personality disorders. Future work could include validation on larger datasets and integration of multimodal clinical data.

items.abstract: Abstract Objective Pakistan has broadened its medical and dental education sphere, yet apprehensions last about undergraduates’ competence, impact of regulation, international acknowledgment of qualifications and retention of the health workforce. This study explored multi stakeholder perspectives on training capacity, quality of education, governance, regulation and acknowledgment of health professions education in Pakistan, and identified prime reforms. Methodology: A qualitative descriptive study was conducted using hybrid focus group discussion held on 4 August 2026 as part of national Health and Education Summit Pakistan (HESP) 2026. Fourteen purposively sampled stakeholders participated in discussion guided by 16 semi structured questions. Data were analysed using Framework Method, and Health Policy Triangle was applied as an interpretive lens. Results Nine themes were identified across three domains. Educational quality and competence : undefined and unenforced competency standards; deficits in clinical training infrastructure; faculty development and continuous quality improvement; and cautious, purpose-specific integration of artificial intelligence. Governance, regulation and recognition : fragmented, input-oriented governance; private-sector representation and public–private imbalance; and international recognition and global alignment. Workforce and equity : equity in workforce planning; and workforce sustainability, security and dignity. Participants identified main barrier to reform is not in an absence of policy but in weak implementation, input based accreditation and poor coordination among regulatory bodies. Conclusion Stakeholders called for a shift from input based to outcome-based accreditation built on a nationally agreed definition of competence, a shared inter agency governance platform, documented clinical supervision and simulation, and workforce protection measures.

items.abstract: Abstract Background Logistic regression remains conventional for identifying correlates of self-reported kidney stone history, but multidimensional comparisons with machine learning—integrating discrimination, calibration, and clinical utility—remain scarce. This study aimed to identify determinants of self-reported kidney stone history among US adults and to compare logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost. Methods We conducted a pooled cross-sectional analysis of six consecutive NHANES cycles (2007–2018), including adults aged ≥ 20 years with complete data on kidney stone history and 16 prespecified candidate predictors. LASSO logistic regression with 10-fold cross-validation selected variables in a 70% training subset. Logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost were trained on the identical predictor set and evaluated on the held-out 30% test set by discrimination (AUC with DeLong's test), calibration (intercept and slope), and clinical utility (decision curve analysis). Survey-weighted sensitivity analysis, collinearity assessment, nomogram, and SHAP analyses. Results Of 25,560 adults, 2,462 (9.6%; survey-weighted 9.99%) reported a lifetime history of kidney stones. LASSO retained 14 of 16 candidates. Eight variables were independently associated with kidney stone history: older age, male sex, lower BMI (inverse), higher waist circumference, elevated blood urea nitrogen, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and current smoking (all 95% CIs excluding unity). BMI and waist circumference showed substantial collinearity (VIFs 7.69 and 7.81). Logistic regression achieved an AUC of 0.644, comparable to XGBoost (0.641; DeLong P = 0.591) and superior to random forest (0.617; P = 0.0005), with the strongest calibration (intercept − 0.147; slope 0.892), followed by XGBoost (slope 0.771) and random forest (slope 0.569). On decision curve analysis, random forest's net benefit fell below the treat-none line within the 15–35% threshold range, whereas logistic regression and XGBoost remained stable. SHAP analysis confirmed age, waist circumference, and blood urea nitrogen as the top contributors; survey-weighted results were consistent. Conclusions Older age, male sex, adiposity-related traits, elevated blood urea nitrogen, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and current smoking were independently associated with prevalent kidney stone history. Logistic regression matched XGBoost in discrimination while showing the best calibration, stable clinical net benefit, and full interpretability. Given the cross-sectional, self-reported design, these findings reflect correlates rather than causal predictors and warrant external validation.

items.abstract: Abstract Objectives: The CARDIO-ML-ED dataset was collected to address the critical shortage of publicly available cardiovascular databases that integrate electrocardiogram (ECG) imagery with comprehensive clinical metadata. Existing ECG repositories lack detailed patient-level information such as laboratory results, vital signs, and medical history—factors essential for developing clinically meaningful machine learning models. We aimed to create a curated, well-labelled, multimodal resource that supports research in automated ECG interpretation, multimodal fusion, and exploratory clinical phenotyping, while promoting reproducibility and innovation in artificial intelligence (AI) driven cardiovascular care. Data description: The CARDIO-ML-ED dataset comprises two complementary components: (1) structured clinical metadata for 582 subjects, and (2) a curated subset of 408 high-resolution ECG images derived from paper-based records digitized through standardized scanning, normalization, cropping, quality filtering, and noise reduction. The dataset includes 82 clinical features per subject—covering demographics, vital signs, laboratory tests (complete blood count, cardiac enzymes, electrolytes, inflammatory markers, arterial blood gases), and medical history. Diagnostic labels were independently assigned by a cardiologist and an emergency medicine physician, achieving substantial interrater agreement (Cohen's kappa = 0.82). This resource offers unique value through its dense integration of ECG data with clinical covariates, enabling multimodal fusion research, unsupervised clustering, imbalanced learning, and predictive analytics.

items.abstract: Asynchronous reinforcement learning increases training throughput, but data from stale policies and numerical mismatch between training and inference can destabilize learning. To stabilize off-policy learning, score centering (SC) removes the effect of reward baselines on the expected update. Our gradient diagnostics show less extreme gradients with SC than with importance sampling (IS), but SC can still fail when the learner moves far from the behavior policy that generated the data. To limit this policy mismatch, we introduce Regularized Score Centering (RSC), which adds a reverse Kullback-Leibler (KL) penalty to encourage the learner's next-token distribution to stay close to the behavior policy's next-token distribution. RSC works with or without truncated importance sampling (TIS), which caps token importance weights. Our theoretical analysis supports this approach, showing that KL regularization improves convergence guarantees. We evaluate dense and mixture-of-experts models on mathematical reasoning and agentic tasks, including online shopping, tool use, games, and fully asynchronous software engineering. RSC with TIS substantially improves sample efficiency across all agentic benchmarks, attaining higher training rewards with the same number of sampled responses. In final evaluations, it achieves top performance across all six agentic tasks, improving by 14.3% on AppWorld and reaching 9.9 times the strongest baseline's score on BabyAI.

items.abstract: Medical image understanding with vision-language models (VLMs) typically relies on autoregressively generating reasoning and answer tokens. These unnecessary tokens make the inference cost scale with the response length and force the answer to be parsed from free-form text, incurring avoidable latency and decision errors. To this end, we introduce MedJev, a system one vision-language decision model that maps medical images, questions, and candidate answers directly to decisions in a single multimodal forward pass, without any autoregressive generation process. For fast inference, MedJev removes the upper language layers and the generative output pathway, while keeping the full vision pathway and all visual tokens. On this shortened backbone, a decision head scores each candidate by pretrained query--key matching and refines the scores with a lightweight multilayer perceptron (MLP) residual, coupling the pretrained matching structure with task-specific nonlinear discrimination. Built on Qwen3.5-4B, MedJev-4B improves both accuracy and speed over the original model on each of four medical image classification and visual question answering benchmarks, with an absolute accuracy gain of 7.93\% and a 6.04times end-to-end speedup. Further comparison with 20 cutting-edge models shows that MedJev-4B achieves state-of-the-art performance and inference speed among 4B--9B general and medical VLMs, indicating that direct multimodal decision making is an effective route to fast and effective medical image understanding.

items.title: ForceHarness: Turning Force into Action and Physics for Frozen Frontier Models
items.summary: Frontier multimodal models can now control robots zero-shot from images, yet many manipulation tasks depend on contact forces that images cannot show. items.abstract: Frontier multimodal models can now control robots zero-shot from images, yet many manipulation tasks depend on contact forces that images cannot show. Bringing force to an API-only frozen model raises two challenges. First, contact evolves much faster than an API model can decide, so the system must close the loop on force beneath the model. Second, a frozen model cannot interpret raw force streams, so force must be returned in a form the model can reason about. Therefore, we present ForceHarness, a harness that lets frozen models use force without demonstrations or finetuning. After calibrating hand force from a wrist sensor or joint torques alone, ForceHarness addresses the first challenge with self-terminating force primitives that regulate force on their own and return at a contact event. To address the second challenge, a physics translation layer turns each force trace into physical quantities with uncertainty as the tool result. To evaluate ForceHarness against expert force controllers and learned policies under identical conditions, we also build HiddenPhys, a seven-task MuJoCo benchmark with hidden physical variables. On a real arm without a wrist force sensor, ForceHarness raises the zero-shot success rate of GPT-6 Astra from 3.3% to 90.0%. In simulation, it adds 17.5 percentage points on the public ForceBench suite and 34.3 percentage points on HiddenPhys, surpassing force-aware policies trained on demonstrations on both benchmarks and matching hand-written expert controllers on HiddenPhys. Ablations further show that smaller models make significantly better decisions when given physical quantities rather than raw force values.

items.abstract: Abstention, the withholding of a response by a large language model (LLM) under uncertainty or safety risks, is essential for trustworthy models. The causes of abstention fall into three perspectives: ambiguity in the Query (Q), limits of Model Knowledge (MK), and misalignment with Human Values (HV). However, prior analyses of internal representations have focused on HV, using a refusal direction computed from harmful and harmless queries. No study has analyzed the three perspectives jointly. We therefore extend the refusal direction framework to all three perspectives. Specifically, for each perspective, we construct counterfactual pairs that share a template and differ only in the abstention-inducing factor, and compute an abstention direction by normalizing the difference in mean activations between the two polarities. Activation steering experiments show that intervening in middle layers increases or decreases abstention across all three perspectives. Moreover, steering yields cross-perspective effects, indicating that the abstention directions share a common directional component.

items.title: Flexible Multi-Stack Super-Resolution of Clinical Brain MRI Using Hetero-Orientation Variational Encoding: Expert Reader Evaluation in a Nigerian Cohort
items.summary: High-resolution brain MRI is important for neuroradiological assessment, yet routine clinical protocols often rely on fast, anisotropic 2D acquisitions, particularly in resource-constrained settings. These acquisitions may differ in orientation, alignment and anatomical coverage, resulting in partially overlapping image stacks. Existing learning-based super-resolution methods typically rely on single,…
items.abstract: High-resolution brain MRI is important for neuroradiological assessment, yet routine clinical protocols often rely on fast, anisotropic 2D acquisitions, particularly in resource-constrained settings. These acquisitions may differ in orientation, alignment and anatomical coverage, resulting in partially overlapping image stacks. Existing learning-based super-resolution methods typically rely on single, under-constrained inputs or fixed multi-stack configurations with idealised acquisition geometry. We introduce MS-HVED, a sequence-agnostic framework for flexible multi-stack brain MRI super-resolution. Available axial, coronal and sagittal stacks are independently encoded into multi-scale Gaussian posteriors and fused using a field-of-view-aware Product-of-Gaussians formulation that limits contributions from unsupported regions. Physics-informed domain randomisation simulates heterogeneous clinical acquisition conditions, including obliqueness, partial coverage and imaging artefacts. MS-HVED achieved competitive or superior reconstruction fidelity across synthetic benchmarks and improved downstream tissue segmentation relative to low-resolution inputs. To assess generalisation beyond the training cohorts, we performed external clinical validation on 30 routine brain MRI examinations from a Nigerian cohort, representing an under-represented population in medical imaging research. These examinations formed the largest component of a blinded reader study involving 44 real cases and seven expert neuroradiologists. In the Nigerian cohort, MS-HVED was preferred over the supervised baseline for overall image quality in 187 of 210 paired assessments. Across all clinical cohorts, MS-HVED achieved higher overall-quality scores with all available inputs (5.93 vs. 4.49, p<.001), with the preference persisting when axial or coronal inputs were omitted (p<.001). Code at github.com/cai4cai/ms-hved

items.abstract: LLM agents answer questions by calling APIs and trusting the results. An API can fail silently. It ignores part of a request, such as a misnamed filter, yet returns HTTP 200 and a plausible but wrong result. Current fixes, such as checklists, reviewer models and LLM judges, ask the model to catch it. But models often see the problem and answer anyway. We present SilentGuard, which moves the decision from the model to the harness running tool calls. It tests each result against invariants that any correct API must satisfy and withholds values that break one. We find silent failures in 11 of 15 public research APIs, with counts inflated up to 691 times. Current fixes leave over 70% of answers wrong, and agents report 77.4% of counts a judge flags. Across 7 open models, SilentGuard cuts wrong answers on its target faults from 74.0% to 1.7%, with no loss on fault-free tasks. On three frontier models they fall from 70.2% to 0.5%. A warning from the same check leaves 70.1% wrong, so enforcement is the key. On new fault types, the harness alone cuts wrong answers from 61.1% to 24.5%. It avoids wrong answers by abstaining rather than recovering.

However, existing agents often answer from common sense instead of reading the evidence. Reinforcement learning (RL) on the final answer cannot correct this, because a guess earns the same reward as reading. items.abstract: Visual agents answer questions about ultra-high-resolution photos by zooming into the relevant regions. However, existing agents often answer from common sense instead of reading the evidence. Reinforcement learning (RL) on the final answer cannot correct this, because a guess earns the same reward as reading. We propose Cross-Input Relative Policy Optimization (CrossRPO), which trains agents on contrast sets. A contrast set asks one question about several versions of an image that differ only in a small region with the evidence and have different answers, so only reading the evidence solves the whole set. CrossRPO rewards solving the whole set, and we prove that it does not reinforce a set answered from common sense. We build contrast sets for training (ViRA-Train) and evaluation (ViRA-Bench) by editing one small object in images of 21 to 120 megapixels, and we photograph further sets with real changes (ViRA-Bench-Real) to exclude editing traces. We train two Visual Reasoning Agents, ViRA-9B and ViRA-27B, with CrossRPO on only about 3,500 items of ViRA-Train each. CrossRPO achieves 63.3% set accuracy on ViRA-Bench at the maximum resolution, against 59.3% for GRPO. ViRA-9B is the most accurate open model of its size on all benchmarks, and ViRA-27B outperforms Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6-Luna, both at their highest thinking level, on most benchmarks.

items.title: LynnReal-Hand: Unlocking World Interaction with Hand Control
items.summary: Interactive video world models enable exploration through text and camera controls, yet direct object interaction requires finer control. Hands provide a natural interface, but translating continuous hand movements into coherent visual responses remains challenging because of complex hand-object dynamics and demanding real-time computation. To address these challenges, we introduce LynnReal-Hand, a hand-controlled…
items.abstract: Interactive video world models enable exploration through text and camera controls, yet direct object interaction requires finer control. Hands provide a natural interface, but translating continuous hand movements into coherent visual responses remains challenging because of complex hand-object dynamics and demanding real-time computation. To address these challenges, we introduce LynnReal-Hand, a hand-controlled video world model that unifies precise interaction modeling with efficient streaming generation. We curate 100K interaction clips spanning diverse real and synthetic environments and develop hand-aware supervision to improve fine-grained hand motions and object interactions. Building on this foundation, we learn a causal flow map for few-step generation and introduce region-aware score distillation that combines complementary video and image priors to refine interaction dynamics and visual appearance. To further reduce inference latency, we propose Ultra-Fast-VAE, a compact video decoder that preserves high reconstruction fidelity with substantially lower computational cost. Extensive evaluations on HandBench demonstrate superior hand-following accuracy and visual quality compared with existing approaches. Our full-sequence model achieves an FVD of 181.67 and a MANO Dice score of 93.02, while the three-step causal model maintains a MANO Dice score of 92.49. For real-time interaction, 540p streaming on a single H200 reaches 18.03 FPS with 741ms latency and an optimized peak GPU memory footprint of only 34.89GB. We will release the datasets, model weights, and the full training and inference code to support research on hand-controlled video world models.

items.title: A Reinforcement Learning Method to Navigate SMEFT Operator Space
items.summary: In particle physics, discrepancies between experimental measurements and Standard Model (SM) predictions are commonly interpreted within new theoretical models. In this context, the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT) provides a general framework encompassing a broad class of models. However, exploring the enormous space of possible SMEFT operators rapidly becomes a challenging combinatorial problem: many…
items.abstract: In particle physics, discrepancies between experimental measurements and Standard Model (SM) predictions are commonly interpreted within new theoretical models. In this context, the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT) provides a general framework encompassing a broad class of models. However, exploring the enormous space of possible SMEFT operators rapidly becomes a challenging combinatorial problem: many operators can contribute simultaneously to different observables, their effects are correlated, and distinct operator combinations can provide comparably good descriptions of the data. In this work, we formulate the exploration of the SMEFT operator space as a sequential decision-making problem using reinforcement learning (RL). Our RL agent employs a lightweight actor-critic architecture with approximately 40K trainable parameters in total. Rather than searching for a single best-fit theory, our method is designed to discover a diverse set of high-quality theory hypotheses. We test the method in a complex phenomenological environment comprising 132 observables across several sectors of particle physics, including 24 measurements that deviate from their SM predictions by more than 1.5σ. We show that the learned RL policy efficiently constructs multi-operator theories that substantially improve the global fit. Comparisons with independent random-subset and random-sequential searches demonstrate the ability of the RL policy to navigate this large combinatorial space. Our results establish RL as a systematic framework for exploring diverse patterns of new physics (NP) interactions within SMEFT.

items.summary: We introduce Sage S1.5 Flash, a 320-billion-parameter general-purpose mixture-of-experts model designed to reason over scientific evidence and act in interactive environments. Sage Sci-Perception uses dedicated encoders for molecular graphs and biological sequences and represents spectra as ordered patches of measurements. Modality-specific projectors map these representations into the input space of a shared…
items.abstract: We introduce Sage S1.5 Flash, a 320-billion-parameter general-purpose mixture-of-experts model designed to reason over scientific evidence and act in interactive environments. Sage Sci-Perception uses dedicated encoders for molecular graphs and biological sequences and represents spectra as ordered patches of measurements. Modality-specific projectors map these representations into the input space of a shared backbone, which processes them alongside text and images. To develop the model's agent capabilities, we construct verifiable environments for tool use, search, and coding, as well as specialized workflows involving machine learning experiments and scientific software. Task completion is checked against execution results, changes in environment state, or submitted artifacts. We evaluate Sage S1.5 Flash on 33 benchmarks across seven domains. In the primary comparison against five baselines, it ranks first on OfficeQA Pro (72.2), MLE-bench Lite (90.3 HumanRank), Harvey LAB, and SpreadsheetBench~2, and second on OSWorld-Verified (85.2), WebArena-Verified (67.6), and DeepResearch Bench~II (54.2). These results show particular strengths in using documentary evidence, producing verifiable workbooks, and carrying out machine learning tasks, alongside competitive performance in desktop and browser workflows that require the model to act on visual feedback.

items.title: InclusionMed: Benchmarking AI for Inclusive Healthcare
items.summary: Advancing medical AI for inclusive healthcare requires evaluation across diverse healthcare roles, tasks, and care settings, but benchmark coverage remains uneven. We introduce InclusionMed, an open medical AI evaluation initiative for inclusive healthcare. The InclusionMed Atlas organizes benchmarks across three healthcare roles and three AI capabilities. For the first release, we selected four public benchmarks…
items.abstract: Advancing medical AI for inclusive healthcare requires evaluation across diverse healthcare roles, tasks, and care settings, but benchmark coverage remains uneven. We introduce InclusionMed, an open medical AI evaluation initiative for inclusive healthcare. The InclusionMed Atlas organizes benchmarks across three healthcare roles and three AI capabilities. For the first release, we selected four public benchmarks from 388 candidates through structured audits and independent reproduction. With InclusionMed-DxFiles, our private diagnostic reasoning benchmark, the Atlas contains five benchmarks covering three of its nine role--capability cells. We evaluated frontier large language models on the Atlas and aggregated their results into the InclusionMed Index, with overall scores ranging from 17.5 to 49.1 out of 100. The Index also reports scores by healthcare role and AI capability, showing that a model's rank varied with the role or capability considered. A within-benchmark analysis using task-level tags showed that the ten highest-ranked models in the Index all scored higher on patient communication than on clinical decision-making. Models with similar Index scores also differed substantially in estimated inference cost. These findings highlight the need for evaluation covering more diverse healthcare needs and for context-specific model selection. Through open collaboration and community contributions, InclusionMed seeks to ensure that diverse healthcare needs worldwide shape how medical AI progress is defined and measured.

items.abstract: Can a vision-language model look at a picture of a chain reaction and tell what will happen? Recent multimodal models describe scenes fluently and solve textbook physics problems, which suggests they should also predict how a scene of ramps, ledges, pendulums, seesaws and dominoes plays out once a ball is pushed. We tested this claim on 30 models from 10 families and reached a clear conclusion: unaided, no model predicts the outcome reliably. We built DominoBench, a benchmark of still images of 2D rigid-body scenes whose outcome a physics simulator computes. It holds 854 items in 427 minimal pairs, in which a change of one to three grid steps in one quantity decides whether one person survives, and every item comes with a four-rung hint ladder ending in the exact calculation that decides the outcome. Unaided, frontier models from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI are right about the person whose fate flips in at most 72% of items and answer both twins of a pair correctly in at most 34%. Pointing at the deciding step helps little, and exact geometry given as text barely helps, yet once the deciding calculation and the quantities it needs, including speeds that a still image cannot show, are written out, the same models reach 82-92% on the deciding person, while small open-weight models stay near chance. Physical prediction from a still image therefore fails at the quantitative step: the strongest models use the deciding quantity when they are given it, but do not produce it on their own. For models that plan or act in the physical world, a fluent account of a scene is thus no evidence of a correct prediction: such models must find and compute the deciding quantity unprompted, and DominoBench tests whether they do.

items.abstract: Application optimization requires coding agents to discover useful changes and coordinate them across a complete program while preserving the required computation. We introduce Accelerate Bench, a benchmark of 32 CPU optimization tasks adapted from scientific applications and supercomputing competitions. Each task provides a working program and specifies the workload, correctness requirements, timing boundaries, and permitted edits, leaving agents to choose where and how to optimize. Public testing supports iterative development, and a separate verifier scores the final submission. On benchmark version 1.1, we evaluate 16 coding agents, each pairing a model with a harness. Their Score@1 ranges from 25.5% to 67.4%. Most of their programs are correct, and the size of the speedup separates them: the two leading agents are at least 2x faster on 22 or more of the 32 tasks, while the other fourteen reach 2x on 8 to 17 and leave 125 of their 412 correct outcomes below 1.25x. Controlled replays show why coordination across an application matters: identical source code runs between 0.29x and 2.12x depending only on build and runtime settings, and one code change is worth 1.01x or 6.4x depending on another. Accelerate Bench pairs executable workloads with agents' programs and trajectories to evaluate both their gains and the process behind them.

items.abstract: Frontier Vision-Language Models (VLMs) such as GPT-6 Astra have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in robot control, suggesting that broad pretraining provides knowledge valuable for physical action. Yet most Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies still rely on much smaller VLM backbones, leaving this potential largely untapped. We ask whether frontier-scale representations can provide a stronger foundation for robot learning. We introduce ScaleVLA, which connects a 552B DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash backbone to a trainable action DiT, and systematically compare VLMs from 2B to 552B under a shared training setup. We evaluate three fundamental capabilities of robot foundation models. In sample efficiency, just 10 demonstrations outperform a 2B backbone trained with 50 (87.8% vs. 85.6%). In generalization, LIBERO-PRO success reaches 45.1%, compared with at most 31.3% for smaller backbones. In precise manipulation, real-world charger insertion improves from 4/10 to 9/10 successes, with gains concentrated in contact-sensitive alignment. Despite its scale, ScaleVLA achieves 216 ms median latency per action chunk. Our findings suggest that frontier VLMs can serve not only as reasoning agents, but also as powerful representational foundations for efficient and generalizable robot policies.

items.abstract: The emergence of multi-omics technologies has enabled the integration of genomic, transcriptomic, epigenomic, proteomic, and metabolomic data to characterize the molecular complexity of cancer. Single-cell and spatial profiling further resolve intratumoral heterogeneity, cell-cell interactions, and the microenvironmental determinants of therapeutic responses. In parallel, artificial intelligence (AI) provides computational approaches for integrating these heterogeneous data types across target identification, drug response prediction, toxicity assessment, and drug-combination modeling. Across these domains, the available evidence indicates that multi-omics integration is most beneficial when the included layers provide complementary biological information; that single-cell and spatial omics analyses reveal treatment-resistant populations and niches but remain largely research-grade and thus not ready for routine clinical deployment; and that although foundation models support some representation-learning tasks, their advantages in perturbation-response prediction require confirmation via stringent evaluation. By distinguishing externally validated advances from retrospective proof-of-concept studies, we provide a practical framework for evaluating the translational readiness of AI-driven multi-omics tools in precision oncology.

items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) holds unprecedented potential to transform the entire Alzheimer's Disease and related dementias (ADRD) research and care continuum. During the 2025 Clinical Trials on Alzheimer's Disease (CTAD) conference, the CTAD Task Force reviewed recent advances in the field, highlighting the emerging role of agentic AI, and discussed priorities to guide future AI-driven innovation in ADRD. Agentic AI co-scientists are emerging as transformative tools to accelerate scientific discovery by autonomously integrating multimodal data, generating and evaluating new hypotheses, and connecting previously siloed knowledge into actionable insights. Operationalized through end-to-end translational pipelines, such platforms can also link mechanistic insights to therapeutic design by automating molecular docking and drug repurposing. Complementary initiatives are creating digital wet labs for in silico experimentation. At the same time, agentic AI is increasingly being used to address pre-discovery bottlenecks by automating data harmonization and inferring missing information through digital twins and synthetic data. AI is also reshaping next-generation ADRD clinical trials, through automated assessment of clinical outcomes, precision participant stratification, individualized disease trajectory modeling and prediction of treatment response. These approaches could substantially improve trial efficiency through responder enrichment. Importantly, AI applications are expanding beyond discovery and clinical trials to support diagnosis, care navigation, and personalized disease management. To translate the momentum surrounding AI innovation into meaningful and sustainable impact across the ADRD continuum, the Task Force identified priorities including the development of AI-ready ecosystems, closer collaboration between clinicians, researchers and computer scientists, AI-enabled optimization of clinical trials and robust ethical and governance frameworks for responsible AI adoption.

items.abstract: Background: The histopathological diagnosis of challenging melanocytic lesions remains limited by substantial interobserver variability. Although computational pathology foundation models demonstrated promising diagnostic performance, their predictions are often difficult to interpret in terms of established criteria. Objective: We evaluated a diagnostic framework combining foundation-model-based whole-slide image analysis, automated prediction of morphological features, and manually assessed PRAME immunohistochemistry. Methods: Using the Virchow2 foundation model and STAMP framework, we analyzed a retrospective cohort of 1,000 melanocytic lesions undergoing PRAME immunohistochemistry. Models were trained on 800 cases and evaluated on a temporally held-out test cohort of 200 cases. Results: The slide-level malignancy classifier achieved a test AUROC of 0.970 (AUPRC 0.984). Separate models predicted established histopathological criteria with high discrimination, including ulceration (AUROC 0.991) and dermal mitoses (AUROC 0.966). In contrast, predicting PRAME expression from H&E images alone showed lower performance (AUROC 0.776-0.780 for PRAME scores 4 and 0). An integrated model combining the slide-level malignancy score, AI-predicted morphological features, and manual PRAME status achieved an AUROC of 0.972 (AUPRC 0.975), comparable to the standalone classifier. In multivariable analysis, PRAME score 4 versus 0 was strongly associated with malignancy (adjusted OR 35.04, 95% CI 17.39-74.62). Conclusions: These findings demonstrate the feasibility of combining foundation-model-based histopathological analysis with established morphological criteria and PRAME immunohistochemistry. Although the integrated framework did not substantially improve overall discrimination, it provides a structured approach for incorporating complementary histopathological and immunohistochemical information into AI-assisted assessment of melanocytic lesions.

items.abstract: Reliable quantitative assessment for chronic total occlusion (CTO) lesions depends on accurate segmentation of coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) images. However, incomplete contrast opacification and complex lesion morphology make precise delineation particularly challenging. We developed an Atrous Attention U-Net (AAU-Net) for CTO segmentation and integrated it into a fully automated workflow comprising heart localization, CTO localization, and lesion segmentation. This retrospective study included 565 CTO lesions from 551 patients who underwent prospectively ECG-gated CCTA at three centers. Standalone segmentation used reference-mask-derived lesion-containing slices and regions of interest, whereas the automated workflow used predicted localization without reference-mask information or manual correction. Under reference-defined localization, AAU-Net achieved a Dice score of 0.8421 and intersection over union of 0.7312 in the internal test set, although performance varied by anatomical location and center. Performance decreased in the fully automated workflow, with Dice scores of 0.6922 in the internal test set, 0.5822 in external test set 1, and 0.6480 in external test set 2, potentially reflecting localization errors and differences between the separately trained segmentation models. In an exploratory locked-model radiomics analysis, features derived from automated segmentations showed numerically lower predictive performance than those derived from manual segmentations. Overall, AAU-Net showed favorable segmentation performance under reference-defined localization, but the fully automated workflow demonstrated lower performance that varied across centers. The radiomics findings demonstrate technical feasibility rather than established clinical utility. Further optimization and larger prospective multicenter validation are required before clinical deployment.

items.abstract: Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics (ST) technologies are recent high-throughput sequencing advancements that enable transcriptome-wide profiling and characterization of cellular populations at single-cell resolution while preserving tissue spatial context. Their integration has been increasingly applied to cancer research, facilitating a deeper understanding of tumor biology and improving diagnostic and therapeutic strategies. Growing evidence suggests that combining single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) with ST offers a robust approach for exploring mechanisms underlying therapeutic resistance. Together, these technologies support the prediction and monitoring of treatment responses and help identify novel therapeutic targets by revealing critical signaling pathways and immune cell populations associated with resistance. Artificial intelligence, including deep learning, computer vision, and generative models, further enhances the integration and analysis of data generated by scRNA-seq and ST, contributing to tumor resistance research. This review summarizes recent advances in the integrated application of scRNA-seq and ST to study tumor resistance and discusses the opportunities, challenges, and future directions of these technologies as a theoretical foundation for identifying therapeutic targets and developing treatment strategies.

items.abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) provides a powerful means to investigate cell fate dynamics during development and disease. However, existing computational approaches-such as RNA velocity-are often limited to qualitative and descriptive insights. We previously presented Dynamo, a machine learning framework that leverages noisy RNA velocity estimates to learn analytical and predictive vector fields of gene expression dynamics. These learned vector fields enable a suite of novel, quantitative analyses, including mapping the geometry of cell state transitions, identifying dynamic features of differentiation trajectories, inferring gene regulatory networks, predicting optimal paths and transcription factor cocktails for cellular reprogramming, and simulating in silico genetic perturbations. Here we provide a comprehensive protocol for applying Dynamo across four distinct data types and five downstream analyses, demonstrating its versatility in handling conventional and metabolic-labeling-enabled scRNA-seq, multiomic datasets and even datasets without velocity information. We also show that Dynamo can predict cell fate diversions following genetic perturbations and accurately identify key transcription factors that enable lineage transitions in the hematopoietic system. By enabling predictive modeling from single-cell data, our protocol aims to empower the development of generative and predictive models of single-cell genomics. While typical RNA velocity vector field analyses can be completed in less than an hour, the nine case studies in the Protocol can be completed in ~7 h and 35 min. The Protocol is designed for researchers with basic familiarity in scRNA-seq analysis and Python programming, although no advanced coding expertise is required.

items.abstract: Jaceosidin exerts protective effects against ulcerative colitis (UC), but its molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood. This study integrates transcriptomics, machine learning, and co-expression network analysis to elucidate Jaceosidin's targets in UC. A dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced mouse colitis model with transcriptome sequencing was established. Core genes were identified by WGCNA and cross-dataset analysis of public UC datasets. Three machine learning algorithms constructed a risk prediction model. GO/KEGG, GSEA, immune infiltration, and single-cell analyses were performed. In vivo validation included enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) for cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-10) and Western blot for core proteins and NF-κB. Two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) explored causality. Forty-one core genes were narrowed to four (CXCL3, LCN2, LMCD1, S100A9) by machine learning. The model achieved AUC > 0.9. GSEA linked the four genes to NF-κB signaling and immune infiltration. ELISA confirmed Jaceosidin reduced TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6 and elevated IL-10. Western blot confirmed NF-κB suppression. MR for LCN2 showed no causal effect on UC risk (p = 0.682), supporting these genes as downstream effectors. Jaceosidin alleviated colitis and downregulated the four genes. Jaceosidin ameliorates UC by modulating a four-gene module and inhibiting NF-κB-mediated inflammation. The model provides new targets for UC treatment monitoring.

items.abstract: The widespread use of metal-based engineered nanoparticles (ENPs) has led to their release into aquatic environments, raising concerns about their potential environmental impact. Despite considerable research to understand the influence of ENPs on phototrophic microorganisms under laboratory settings, their influences on natural communities remain poorly understood, and this gap has not yet been comprehensively reviewed. By integrating the current knowledge across laboratory and field studies, this review critically examines how the effect of ENPs on phototrophic microorganisms propagate across ecological scales, from individual organisms to natural communities. ENPs toxicity towards phototrophic microorganisms depends on water physico-chemical characteristics and intrinsic properties of ENPs. Cellular traits and taxonomic identities strongly influence ENPs toxicity, with smaller cells and cyanobacteria being more prone to adverse effects than large species and other taxa. The selective toxicity of ENPs can reshape natural communities without necessarily reducing their total biomass. This may result in the dominance of opportunistic species, decreasing species diversity and making communities more vulnerable to environmental disturbances. Consequently, ENPs may trigger cascading effects on biogeochemical cycles and food webs, that could be further intensified by climate change. This review further identifies critical methodological limitations in assessing the sensitivity of natural communities to ENPs and emphasises the importance of using recent analytical techniques, such as single-cell techniques, machine learning and omics techniques, to overcome these challenges. Improving our understanding of ENPs toxicity towards natural communities is therefore essential for accurately assessing their ecological risk assessment.

items.abstract: Visible artifacts are an unreliable cue for detecting generated videos, because newer generators learn to remove them. We instead detect a trace left by the generation pipeline itself. Most video generators decode latents with a 3D causal VAE that groups consecutive frames in time, so the fidelity of generated frames rises and falls periodically with their position in a group. We call this periodic trace VAE Rhythm. Real videos are captured frame by frame and do not have it. To reveal it without training, we propose a phase scan. The scan reconstructs a clip with an off-the-shelf VAE from successive start offsets and measures the periodicity of the reconstruction error across these offsets. We find VAE Rhythm in most of the 39 variants of 31 generators we test, including the closed-source Sora, Kling 3.0 and Seedance 2.0. We use the rhythm as a zero-shot score, as a plug-in for existing detectors and as a data engine that pairs real videos with their VAE reconstructions to train our detector CaDet. On DF26, the training-free rhythm score outperforms all 15 retrained baselines, and as a plug-in it improves all 19 tested detectors by 6.7% to 23.7% AUROC. CaDet achieves the best AUROC on AIGVDBench, DF26 and three 2026 closed-source models, and its variant trained without any generated video still exceeds 90% on AIGVDBench.

items.abstract: Streaming video LLMs can continuously observe the world, yet often handle user requests in isolation. We introduce ALIVE, an interactive streaming video model supporting proactive monitoring, streaming task coordination, and feedback-seeking interaction. We construct ALIVE-SFT-288K and ALIVE-RL-3K for two-stage training. Contrastive supervised fine-tuning teaches when and how to respond, while reinforcement learning with Behavior-Aligned Credit Assignment (BACA) combines trajectory-level and local advantages to refine decisions, responses, and silence across multi-turn interactions. We also introduce FSI-Bench to evaluate feedback seeking and subsequent task completion. ALIVE achieves the highest overall scores among the compared models on four public benchmarks and FSI-Bench, demonstrating strong streaming understanding and interactive capabilities.

items.title: CONGA: Compiling Gaussian Fiber Geometry for Structured Bayesian Inference

items.abstract: In structured Bayesian models, a large latent block is often Gaussian conditional on a smaller set of parameters, yet generic inference methods relearn this geometry during warmup. We study how this structure can be used to construct transports for posterior inference. The conditional mean and precision determine exact affine maps, including symmetric Brenier and triangular Knothe-Rosenblatt maps, that separate a standard normal block from the remaining non-Gaussian core. KL and relative Fisher objectives then reduce to objectives on this core. We introduce CONGA, a compiler that identifies candidate Gaussian blocks and selects a temporal, spectral, or sparse implementation according to their structure and computational cost. Marginalization requires an identity established from the model; numerical evidence alone permits only a target-preserving change of variables, and a failed check leaves the model unchanged. On the Stock-Watson inflation model, CONGA improves minimum ESS per second by 12.5x for NUTS. It also restores convergence where the raw target fails: for WALNUTS on the same model, and for NUTS on a 6760-dimensional electricity load model reduced to 34 core coordinates. Experiments on graph-indexed fields show how coloring and fill affect the choice of map, including cases where retaining the original target is preferable. Code at https://github.com/vicgalle/conga

items.summary: Speculative-diffusion decoding uses a small parallel drafter model to generate b draft tokens in one forward pass, which then undergo parallel verification via a larger target model. Faster inference can be achieved when multiple draft tokens pass verification simultaneously. Recent parallel draft architectures (DFlash, DSpark) improve draft quality by conditioning on rich features computed by the target, through a…
items.abstract: Speculative-diffusion decoding uses a small parallel drafter model to generate b draft tokens in one forward pass, which then undergo parallel verification via a larger target model. Faster inference can be achieved when multiple draft tokens pass verification simultaneously. Recent parallel draft architectures (DFlash, DSpark) improve draft quality by conditioning on rich features computed by the target, through a mechanism known as feature encoding. However, standard feature encoding mechanisms have three limitations: (1) they are lossy, applying encoding projections that are destructive to the underlying target feature-space via a discovered effect known as residual mixing, (2) they are memory-less, with no record of previously processed proposals, and (3) they utilize features sampled uniformly from across the target layers, omitting important hidden states. To address these issues, we propose Mixture-of-Features Attention (MoFA), a lightweight feature-encoding approach equipped with a working memory that encodes previously rejected proposals. Leveraging MoFA, rejection memory, and a set of further enhancements, including 2-tap causal convolutions, prefix-only cross-attention, and non-uniform target layer selection, the final architecture, DNeo, achieves 1.3x faster generation speed than SoTA (DFlash-2) without impacting drafter footprint or generation quality. DNeo marks a new state of the art in high quality, fast LLM inference.

items.title: HubEgo-100K: In-the-Wild Egocentric Video of Skilled Work for Robot Learning
items.summary: Robot policies trained by imitation generalize poorly outside the environments and objects seen in training. Published data-scaling studies find that generalization grows with the diversity of training environments and objects rather than with more demonstrations per environment. Robot data is costly to collect across many environments, whereas egocentric human video can be recorded in the wild at scale; existing…
items.abstract: Robot policies trained by imitation generalize poorly outside the environments and objects seen in training. Published data-scaling studies find that generalization grows with the diversity of training environments and objects rather than with more demonstrations per environment. Robot data is costly to collect across many environments, whereas egocentric human video can be recorded in the wild at scale; existing egocentric video, however, mostly shows daily-life activity and contains little skilled work in real workplaces. We present HubEgo-100K, a dataset built for diversity. This version of the paper covers the first release, v1.0: 10,124 hours of 1080p egocentric video with synchronized 100 Hz inertial (IMU) data from one head-mounted phone camera. In v1.0, 12,227 contributors record their own unscripted work in 15,548 environments (each one contributor's own setting of one type, such as their kitchen or workshop) across 11 setting types, 30 work categories, 56 task types and 35 action families, with 83% of hours in workplace settings. The release comprises 72,754 episodes with machine-generated action and language annotations, in LeRobot and MCAP formats under CC BY 4.0. We measure diversity along each axis, show that inside v1.0, with episodes in random order, new contributors and words keep appearing, and relate the measurements to published evidence on six data properties tied to policy performance, including hand visibility and inertial sensing. We also document collection, curation, privacy measures and data format, and provide a datasheet. Later versions of this paper will add benchmarks and cover further releases toward 100,000 hours.

items.title: VisualArtifactSpec 1.0: Evaluating Visual Artifacts under Task Specifications
items.summary: Visual artifact tasks test agents' ability to translate task specifications and source materials into outputs that meet practical needs. Evaluation across artifact families helps distinguish broadly applicable authoring capabilities from strengths confined to a particular medium. We introduce VisualArtifactSpec 1.0 (VAS), a benchmark of 211 creation and modification tasks spanning presentations, static graphics,…
items.abstract: Visual artifact tasks test agents' ability to translate task specifications and source materials into outputs that meet practical needs. Evaluation across artifact families helps distinguish broadly applicable authoring capabilities from strengths confined to a particular medium. We introduce VisualArtifactSpec 1.0 (VAS), a benchmark of 211 creation and modification tasks spanning presentations, static graphics, animations and videos, and web interfaces. Each task specifies authoring objectives, source materials, constraints, and deliverables. Existing benchmarks provide limited support for systematically evaluating how authoring choices suit different audiences, purposes, and media across artifact families. VAS evaluates two aspects separately: Task Fulfillment verifies explicit requirements and applicable functionality, while Artifact Performance assesses Content, Organization, Visuals, and Delivery. Task-specific rating anchors instantiate shared criteria for the intended audience, purpose, and medium, with judgments grounded in source materials and artifact inspection records. We evaluate nine model-harness configurations on all 211 tasks. Overall scores range from 42.12 to 70.52, with Artifact Performance accounting for 73.4% of the gap between the highest- and lowest-scoring configurations.

items.title: AuXSpec: Learning to Autoformalize Program Specifications via Executable Postconditions
items.summary: Formal specifications define intended program behavior and underpin verification, but writing them in theorem provers such as Lean is slow and expertise-intensive, making specification a major bottleneck to scaling formally correct code. Autoformalization from natural-language problems is promising, yet training specification models requires scalable feedback on whether generated specifications capture intended…
items.abstract: Formal specifications define intended program behavior and underpin verification, but writing them in theorem provers such as Lean is slow and expertise-intensive, making specification a major bottleneck to scaling formally correct code. Autoformalization from natural-language problems is promising, yet training specification models requires scalable feedback on whether generated specifications capture intended behavior. Prior approaches obtain this feedback through explicit proofs or separately implemented code with formal correspondence proofs, both expensive. We introduce AuXSpec, a Lean framework that pairs declarative postconditions with executable counterparts, obtained through type class resolution when possible and otherwise defined separately with an equivalence proof. Test cases can then evaluate declarative specifications by execution, letting us use agreement as a reinforcement-learning reward. Using AuXSpec, we synthesize 3,037 LeetCode problems and expand training to 19.5K samples through expert iteration on Codeforces. Experiments show that training Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.8-27B with the execution-based reward improves SpecGen pass@4 on AuXSpec-Test 0.7% to 82.7% and 14.3% to 84.3%, and the 27B model outperforms all frontier models. On the out-of-domain Verina benchmark with its original prompts, both models improve 7.0% to 90.5% and 21.9% to 90.5% and surpass VeriSpecGen-30B-A3B, the prior state of the art among open-source specification models, on pass@1 (theirs 47.6% vs. ours 73.7% and 84.5%) and pass@4 (theirs 63.9% at pass@10 vs. ours 90.5%). We release the weights of the trained 9B and 27B models and the 3,037 problems with test cases, including the 300-problem AuXSpec-Test benchmark with expert review and correctness proofs for future evaluation. Models and data: https://huggingface.co/collections/eth-algopt/auxspec. Website: https://auxspec.org

items.title: VideoNexus: Video Perception Beyond the Reasoning Context
items.summary: Understanding long videos requires locating evidence, resolving visual details, and integrating observations into an answer. Even when relevant evidence is present, performing these operations within long, dense visual sequences burdens both perception and reasoning. Video agents enable selective inspection, but returning frames to the planner still accumulates visual information in its reasoning context. Delegating…
items.abstract: Understanding long videos requires locating evidence, resolving visual details, and integrating observations into an answer. Even when relevant evidence is present, performing these operations within long, dense visual sequences burdens both perception and reasoning. Video agents enable selective inspection, but returning frames to the planner still accumulates visual information in its reasoning context. Delegating perception reduces this burden, yet sparse sampling can miss decisive details, and per-frame descriptions can preserve context growth. We introduce VideoNexus, a training-free framework that separates detailed video perception from evidence-driven planning and reasoning. The planner controls where to inspect, what to resolve, and how densely to sample. Perception sub-agents process native audio-video in independent contexts and return compact, temporally grounded evidence for iterative search and verification. Using Gemini 3.8 Flash for both planning and perception, VideoNexus achieves 88.6% accuracy on full LVBench, exceeding same-backbone static ingestion and built-in agentic processing by 3.6 and 1.1 points, respectively, at 44% of the latter's measured API cost. A paired LVBench subset ablation shows lower planner input and higher accuracy. With Kimi K3 as the shared backbone, VideoNexus improves over the official Video-GAIA ReAct harness by 8.5 points in our evaluation. These results support compact evidence exchange for combining detailed observation with efficient planning and reasoning.

items.title: The Mask Is Not the Object: Volumetric Supervision for 3D Gaussian Segmentation
items.summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting enables object-level operations on Gaussian primitives, yet existing segmentation methods are largely trained and evaluated through rendered views. This mismatch can produce accurate rendered masks from incomplete 3D selections since alpha-blended feature supervision concentrates learning on dominant contributors while leaving occluded or low-contribution Gaussians weakly supervised. We propose…
items.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting enables object-level operations on Gaussian primitives, yet existing segmentation methods are largely trained and evaluated through rendered views. This mismatch can produce accurate rendered masks from incomplete 3D selections since alpha-blended feature supervision concentrates learning on dominant contributors while leaving occluded or low-contribution Gaussians weakly supervised. We propose VODA, a plug-and-play supervision objective that exploits local depth structure to group per-pixel contributors and directly supervises all Gaussians in selected depth clusters, bypassing contribution-weighted gradient delivery. To evaluate volumetric completeness, we introduce Removal-3D, a synthetic object-removal benchmark, and the Removal Depth Error (RDE), a metric comparing predicted and ground-truth depth changes. Across four rendering-based baselines, VODA consistently improves volumetric segmentation on Removal-3D while maintaining or improving performance on LERF and ScanNet. Further analysis shows that VODA recovers lower-contribution Gaussians, while simple gradient reweighting and spatial propagation fail to reproduce comparable gains.

items.title: WeVisForensics: Self-Evolving Agent for Omni AI-Generated Video Detection
items.summary: Recent advances in video generation call for reliable detection grounded in explicit forensic evidence. However, current methods primarily depend on single-pass chain-of-thought reasoning that overlooks brief or localized artifacts, or on predefined multi-agent workflows that offer limited flexibility in selecting relevant inspections. Even with adaptive investigation, optimizing the investigation policy alone does…
items.abstract: Recent advances in video generation call for reliable detection grounded in explicit forensic evidence. However, current methods primarily depend on single-pass chain-of-thought reasoning that overlooks brief or localized artifacts, or on predefined multi-agent workflows that offer limited flexibility in selecting relevant inspections. Even with adaptive investigation, optimizing the investigation policy alone does not directly improve the forensic capabilities of fixed experts. We introduce WeVisForensics, an agentic framework in which a main investigator agent coordinates a self-evolving library of forensic inspector sub-agents spanning visual and audio cues. The investigator learns which artifact type to examine, over which window, and when to conclude, and these interactions provide shared feedback for both levels of agents. Our dual-timescale policy optimization strategy, DTPO, closes this loop through fast reinforcement learning of the investigator and slower refinement of the inspectors, guided by annotated artifact intervals, to report subtle artifacts they once dismissed. Furthermore, we curate ForenCue-30K, combining role-specific forensic annotations and interaction trajectories to supervise individual inspections and their coordination, with an accompanying reinforcement-learning pool. Experiments show that WeVisForensics averages 95.2% detection accuracy across in-domain, out-of-domain and agentic benchmarks, 9.0% above the strongest prior detector, while grounding its verdicts in localized evidence.

items.title: BLIP-Live: Balancing Timeliness & Firing Precision in Proactive Streaming Video Agents
items.summary: Streaming video understanding is becoming increasingly important for real-world interactive systems. Such systems must be proactive for natural and useful human interaction: they should respond as soon as sufficient evidence becomes available while avoiding premature, redundant, or incorrect responses. We present BLIP-Live, a framework unifying data, metrics, harness, and training around a shared formulation of…
items.abstract: Streaming video understanding is becoming increasingly important for real-world interactive systems. Such systems must be proactive for natural and useful human interaction: they should respond as soon as sufficient evidence becomes available while avoiding premature, redundant, or incorrect responses. We present BLIP-Live, a framework unifying data, metrics, harness, and training around a shared formulation of proactivity as effective causal response decisions balancing the two competing objectives of responding vs silence. First, we construct BLIP-Live-780K dataset containing human annotations of proactive response content and timing, which defines this desired behavior. We then propose PAUC-F, a metric to effectively measure our desired proactive behavior. PAUC-F combines existing response timeliness metrics with firing precision to reward early useful responses without rewarding excessive firing. With our desired behavior defined and measurable, we finally investigate model-agnostic inference harnesses that draw out proactive streaming capabilities of offline vision language models (VLMs), together with training pipelines that learn to further improve their proactive responsiveness. Across both settings, we find that combinations of sliding visual windows, online interaction memory, and structured response outputs consistently yield strongest proactive performance. Our experiments result in two models, with our BLIP-Live-Qwen model achieving state-of-the-art performance across four proactive streaming benchmarks, with gains up to 44% over baselines and outperforming multiple closed API models. Our code and data will be released publicly.

items.title: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights
items.summary: Language models are trained once, frozen and deployed: improving one again takes another training run, and a prompt, a scaffold or extra computation at inference is gone once the task ends. A frontier model has been shown to edit the weights of a much smaller one. We ask whether a model can rewrite its own weights to make itself better, and find that it can, by its own reasoning, with no gradients and no training;…
items.abstract: Language models are trained once, frozen and deployed: improving one again takes another training run, and a prompt, a scaffold or extra computation at inference is gone once the task ends. A frontier model has been shown to edit the weights of a much smaller one. We ask whether a model can rewrite its own weights to make itself better, and find that it can, by its own reasoning, with no gradients and no training; we call this self-rewriting. Given its weights, graded answers and the ability to run itself, a 27B model diagnoses its failure and edits the weights behind it. It surpasses itself: its own edit makes it 6.6 points more accurate on 490 problems it never saw, in a test fixed in advance, and another session's edit also makes it significantly better. It keeps getting better: it submits an edit only when its own tests support it, each edit replacing the last, and over its first eight such sessions its accuracy only rises. Unlike test-time scaling, the gain persists in its weights and adds no cost per answer; unlike training, it needs no pre- or post-training infrastructure, only an open model and hours on one GPU. It repairs a damaged copy of itself: it locates the corrupted matrix and rewrites it with values of its own, never reading the undamaged weights; found on text math problems alone, the repair lifts the copy on six image benchmarks it never saw from 7% to 70% accuracy, 83% of the undamaged model's. And the ability emerges with scale: across four sizes of one family, the 2B model makes no edit and the 4B and 9B models break themselves; only the 27B model works on itself as a human would, comparing its hidden states on answers that finish and on answers that run out of tokens, weakening the direction that separates them. Like a human, a model need not separate training from inference; improving a language model may come to take a conversation rather than a training run.

Local LLMs hallucinate, and an invented value in a tool call propagates through every later step. Here we present a method to build System 1 agents: local agents that call tools without generating text. A deterministic compiler turns each…
items.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence could automate analyses of sensitive clinical data, but current agents depend on large language models (LLMs). Cloud LLMs expose patient data. Local LLMs hallucinate, and an invented value in a tool call propagates through every later step. Here we present a method to build System 1 agents: local agents that call tools without generating text. A deterministic compiler turns each tool's schema and the request into multiple-choice questions whose options come from the request and the schema, then a one-pass decision model answers them. On 1,952 requests to 157 biomedical tools, the best System 1 agent chose the right tool, or correctly declined, for 97.0% of requests, significantly ahead of all 18 local LLM-agent settings (best 95.2%). The System 1 agent filled 97.0% of 6,056 stated argument values. No System 1 call contained invented content, against 5.5-19.7% of LLM calls. The System 1 Agents framework is freely available as open-source software at https://github.com/eltzanis/SystemOneAgents.

items.abstract: Code-search benchmarks show dense encoders well ahead of BM25, yet coding agents do well with grep. What does this dense advantage measure? Existing benchmarks cannot tell: they use curated queries, old code and a handicapped BM25. To find out, we build Repo-Premium, a realistic repository-level code-search benchmark. It ranks files in real repositories, with curated and raw queries in Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Go, Rust and Java, pull requests from 2022 to 2026, and a preregistered test pool over 91 repositories. Our experiments trace the advantage to two sources: evaluation choices that favor dense retrieval, such as splitting files into chunks for BM25 and counting edited tests as relevant, and queries that lack the code's rare identifiers. Expanding the query with LLM-written identifiers (generate-then-grep) helps BM25 far more than dense retrieval, letting it match dense retrieval in every Python pool, even on pull requests opened after the LLM was released. No method we tried predicts which retriever will win on a given query. From these results we derive three guidelines: measure dense gains against a fair lexical baseline, fuse dense retrieval with BM25, and add the code's words to queries that lack them.

items.abstract: Background Rib cage remodeling procedures, like rib osteotomy with osteosynthesis, have shown promise for waist narrowing in aesthetic surgery. However, the ideal osteotomy location and bending angle remain poorly defined. Objectives This preclinical, proof-of-concept study aimed to: (1) quantify how osteotomy location and rib bending angle affect rib apex displacement using a large, computed tomography (CT) dataset, and (2) develop a data-driven framework as a first step toward guiding selection of rib number, osteotomy site, and bending angle tailored to individual waist contour goals. Methods Using the open-source RibFrac CT dataset, 600 ribs (300 eleventh [XI] and 300 tenth [X]) were segmented with the RibSeg deep learning tool. A custom MATLAB script simulated 15 bending scenarios per rib by varying osteotomy location (7 cm, 8 cm, 9 cm from midline) and bending angles (10°, 20°, 30°, 45°, 55°). Displacement at the rib apex was computed using a chord-perpendicular method. A graphical user interface (GUI) allowed for manual interaction, and a linear mixed-effects model quantified the effects of angle, osteotomy location, and their interaction. Results Both bending angle and osteotomy distance significantly affected apex displacement (p < 0.001), with a negative interaction indicating reduced effect of angle at more lateral osteotomy points. Rib X showed greater displacement overall than rib XI. Conclusions This proof-of-concept model establishes a biomechanical foundation for individualized rib remodeling planning. While prospective clinical validation is needed, the framework is adaptable to patient-specific imaging across age, sex, and BMI, and may ultimately support personalized surgical decision-making.
