items.abstract: Nontuberculous mycobacterial lung disease (NTM-LD) is highly heterogeneous, geographically and etiologically, hindering effective timely identification. Prior CT radiomics studies require manual segmentation of pathology. We developed a whole-lung CT radiomics-based machine learning approach and identified common features across two geographically distinct NTM-LD cohorts. We included 1,300 chest CT scans from China (871 TB; 429 NTM, Dataset 1) and 173 independent NTM cohort from the University of Alabama at Birmingham (UAB), US. Whole-lung regions were automatically segmented on each scan, and 85 quantitative radiomic features were extracted using a standardized image-processing pipeline. We evaluated two frameworks to assess model performance and generalizability: (1) training on Dataset 1 with external validation on Dataset 2, and (2) training on the combined cohort. Linear discriminant analysis (LDA) was used as the primary classification method. Cross-cohort concordance analysis was performed to evaluate the reproducibility of radiomic features across datasets. In Scenario 1, the LDA classifier trained on Dataset 1 achieved an AUC of 0.79 (95% CI, 0.73-0.84) with high specificity (0.91). On the external UAB cohort, the model achieved an AUC of 0.94 (95% CI, 0.90-0.97). In Scenario 2, the combined cohort model achieved an AUC of 0.81 (95% CI, 0.76-0.85) with improved sensitivity (0.61) and precision (0.82). Feature importance analysis identified 16 features consistently ranked among the top 20 in both scenarios, predominantly texture-based descriptors reflecting distinct parenchymal patterns between mycobacterial species. In conclusion, whole-lung CT radiomics enables interpretable NTM-LD classification across geographically distinct populations without manual annotation. Suggesting population-independent parenchymal signatures of NTM-LD.

items.summary: Objective This retrospective, multicenter study evaluated whether MRI-based radiomics can predict the histological response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy in Ewing sarcoma patients and compared their performance to that of radiological findings. Definitive histological assessment is only possible during surgery, potentially delaying therapy changes and increasing metastatic risk; therefore, a positive outcome would…
items.abstract: Objective This retrospective, multicenter study evaluated whether MRI-based radiomics can predict the histological response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy in Ewing sarcoma patients and compared their performance to that of radiological findings. Definitive histological assessment is only possible during surgery, potentially delaying therapy changes and increasing metastatic risk; therefore, a positive outcome would enable early adaptations. Methods Radiomics features were extracted from pre- and post-neoadjuvant (after first chemotherapy cycle) chemotherapy scans of patients treated from 2004 to 2020. Four machine learning models were trained using nested cross-validation to predict histological response, and their performance was compared to models trained on semantic features derived from expert radiological readings. Diagnostic performance was measured by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC). Results 96 patients (mean age, 19.9 ± 11.7 years; 41 women) with Ewing sarcoma were evaluated. Radiomics features related to low gray level intensity changes in T1 fat-saturated contrast-enhanced sequences showed the highest responder identification performance (AUROC, 0.62; 95% CI: 0.59, 0.65), surpassing the best radiological model, which relied on the relative change in maximum diameter of extratumoral soft tissue components (AUROC, 0.58; 95% CI: 0.56, 0.60). Radiomics models relying on pre-treatment T2-weighted data performed similarly (AUROC, 0.61; 95% CI: 0.58, 0.64), outperforming the clinical baseline (AUROC, 0.53; 95% CI: 0.51, 0.55). Conclusion MRI-based radiomics moderately identified responders to neoadjuvant chemotherapy, suggesting a role for earlier, tailored therapeutic strategies in Ewing sarcoma. Larger studies to validate these findings within a multimodal framework are warranted. Clinical relevance statement Radiomics extracted from MRI scans may aid with non-size tissue signals in early prediction of neoadjuvant chemotherapy response in Ewing sarcoma patients, potentially guiding personalized treatment adaptations, reducing delays for non-responders, and improving patient outcomes. These exploratory findings are complementary to standard size-based assessment from clinical routine, and warrant larger, prospective trials to be established.

items.summary: Learning whole-body mobile manipulation requires demonstrations that coordinate bimanual actions with locomotion across extended workspaces. However, existing interfaces trade off direct robot control, perception and action alignment, and natural operator mobility, making such demonstrations difficult to collect. We introduce HALO, a human-aligned data collection system for whole-body mobile manipulation. The system…
items.abstract: Learning whole-body mobile manipulation requires demonstrations that coordinate bimanual actions with locomotion across extended workspaces. However, existing interfaces trade off direct robot control, perception and action alignment, and natural operator mobility, making such demonstrations difficult to collect. We introduce HALO, a human-aligned data collection system for whole-body mobile manipulation. The system aligns the operator's perception and action space with the robot while preserving direct physical feedback and natural locomotion. Operators guide the robot end-effectors through kinesthetic teaching and move a low-resistance platform without the deployed mobile base while performing bimanual manipulation. This interface enables more natural whole-body demonstrations, but the close human-robot coupling introduces discrepancies between the demonstration and deployment settings. We address these discrepancies with deployment-aligned demonstration processing, which calibrates and temporally aligns platform motion with the deployed base response and masks and inpaints demonstrator hands in recorded observations. Compared with Mobile ALOHA and VR teleoperation, HALO enables up to 2.9x faster demonstration collection while maintaining comparable or higher success rates. Policies trained with HALO perform precise manipulation tasks, including zip-tie fastening, and achieve a 73.3% success rate on a six-stage long-horizon mobile manipulation task involving repeated coordinated base and arm motion. Project page: https://robbyant-research.github.io/Lingbot-ALOHA/

items.title: Reducing Batch Makespan for LLM Agent Workloads through Inference-Environment Coordination
items.summary: Efficient batch execution of agent tasks is critical to LLM training and development workflows, including benchmark evaluation, synthetic-data generation, and RL rollouts. Since these tasks alternate between LLM inference and environment interaction, we present coordinated optimizations to reduce batch makespan, the time required to complete all tasks in a batch. For hybrid LLMs, a workload-based resource model…
items.abstract: Efficient batch execution of agent tasks is critical to LLM training and development workflows, including benchmark evaluation, synthetic-data generation, and RL rollouts. Since these tasks alternate between LLM inference and environment interaction, we present coordinated optimizations to reduce batch makespan, the time required to complete all tasks in a batch. For hybrid LLMs, a workload-based resource model guides GPU-memory allocation between key-value (KV) cache and recurrent state and provides a reference sample concurrency to exploit parallelism while limiting recomputation. Trajectory-aware routing and scheduling promote cache reuse while balancing worker load. Under constrained environment capacity, we decouple sample admission from environment execution and introduce Chain-Advancing Action Scheduling (CAAS), which prioritizes long chains using observed progress to shorten the batch tail. Controlled replay combines actual inference with recorded environment responses and durations for ablations of individual optimizations. Live evaluations with Ling-3.0-Flash and Ling-3.1-Flash on the BFCL, SWE-bench Multilingual, WideSearch, and MCP-Atlas benchmarks demonstrate makespan reductions of 10.4% to 65.0%, while evaluation scores remain aligned. Furthermore, these methods have been successfully applied to training and evaluation workflows for the Ling-3.x model series, accelerating the model-development cycle.

items.summary: Given a set of LEGO parts and an image of an assembled object, our task is to infer the pose of each part to assemble the object. In contrast with traditional 3D reconstruction, doing so requires satisfying discrete physical constraints, which provide structure but render the problem combinatorial and highly sensitive to small pose errors. To learn a prior over how parts fit together, we train a set-conditioned…
items.abstract: Given a set of LEGO parts and an image of an assembled object, our task is to infer the pose of each part to assemble the object. In contrast with traditional 3D reconstruction, doing so requires satisfying discrete physical constraints, which provide structure but render the problem combinatorial and highly sensitive to small pose errors. To learn a prior over how parts fit together, we train a set-conditioned SE(3) flow model on procedurally generated assemblies. We then finetune this model to inject image conditioning, using 1% as much data. However, while the learned flow captures global structure, it does not enforce connectivity. To address this, we introduce an analytic connectivity-field guidance to pull predictions toward connected assemblies at test time. Through this, we demonstrate improved build quality with model size, pretraining, and guidance. We make our models and data available for research purposes at https://kulits.github.io/BrickFlow/

items.title: Dual Flow: Joint Image-Measurement Interpolation for Inverse Problems
items.summary: Generative model-based approaches to linear inverse problems typically use the acquired noisy measurement to condition or guide sampling in the image domain. In this work, we introduce Dual Flow, a novel joint-flow model for solving linear inverse problems by jointly estimating the clean image and corresponding noise-free measurement from the observation. Specifically, Dual Flow formulates image reconstruction and…
items.abstract: Generative model-based approaches to linear inverse problems typically use the acquired noisy measurement to condition or guide sampling in the image domain. In this work, we introduce Dual Flow, a novel joint-flow model for solving linear inverse problems by jointly estimating the clean image and corresponding noise-free measurement from the observation. Specifically, Dual Flow formulates image reconstruction and measurement denoising as a coupled estimation problem, using coupled flows in the image and measurement domains. The acquired noisy measurement is used only to initialize the measurement state; thereafter, image and measurement states are jointly updated based on their current values. By construction, the final image and measurement estimates are guaranteed to satisfy the underlying forward model. We derive the sampling updates for the joint-flow which involves the conditional mean of the clean image given the joint state. We further derive a closed-form expression for a sufficient statistic of the joint state and show that the required conditional mean can be obtained by solving an image-domain Gaussian denoising problem involving operator-dependent, correlated noise. We train a velocity-prediction network using this formulation to estimate the conditional mean from the derived sufficient statistic. Extensive experiments across various linear inverse problems and image datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in both distortion metrics and perceptual quality. Dual Flow requires no hyperparameter tuning beyond the number of inference steps and achieves shorter reconstruction times than competing methods. Additional analyses assess robustness to model mismatch, as well as the ability to generate diverse plausible reconstructions and characterize reconstruction uncertainty.

items.title: EvenVLM: A Text and Multimodal Dataset for the Even Language with Vision-Language Fine-Tuning
items.summary: We present EvenVLM, the first text and multimodal (VQA) dataset for Even (Lamut), an endangered Northern Tungusic language spoken by approximately 6,800 people in Siberia. Our dataset comprises 50,521 structured Even-Russian entries extracted from dictionary and phrasebook sources via GPT-4o Mini-based parsing, from which we synthetically generate 107,543 training examples spanning translation, grammar, reading…
items.abstract: We present EvenVLM, the first text and multimodal (VQA) dataset for Even (Lamut), an endangered Northern Tungusic language spoken by approximately 6,800 people in Siberia. Our dataset comprises 50,521 structured Even-Russian entries extracted from dictionary and phrasebook sources via GPT-4o Mini-based parsing, from which we synthetically generate 107,543 training examples spanning translation, grammar, reading comprehension, and semantic classification. To address tokenization inefficiency on Even's agglutinative morphology, we propose a three-step tokenizer expansion algorithm that adds Even-specific graphemes (eng, oe, o-umlaut), whitelisted vocabulary, and BPE merges, reducing average tokens per word by 27% (4.99 to 3.64). Using LoRA fine-tuning of Qwen3-VL-4B, we adapt the model for text tasks (0.53% trainable parameters, rank 32) and separately for visual question answering (rank 64, frozen vision encoder). Our best configuration achieves 11.4% exact match and a 13.6 weighted score on text benchmarks, 0.1283 chrF for sentence translation, and 65% accuracy on VQA (up from 0% for the base model and text-only fine-tuning). We release our datasets, evaluation benchmarks, and training pipeline to support further research on Even and other low-resource languages.

items.title: Alloy: A Multi-Material Physics Engine for Robot Learning
items.summary: Robots handle much more than rigid objects: towels, cables, water, sand. The simulators used to train robots at scale are strongest on rigid bodies, and adding another material usually means a second engine and hand-written glue between the two. We present Alloy, an open-source physics engine for robot learning in which rigid robots, cloth, cables, liquids, granular material and soft bodies share one scene. Each…
items.abstract: Robots handle much more than rigid objects: towels, cables, water, sand. The simulators used to train robots at scale are strongest on rigid bodies, and adding another material usually means a second engine and hand-written glue between the two. We present Alloy, an open-source physics engine for robot learning in which rigid robots, cloth, cables, liquids, granular material and soft bodies share one scene. Each object is described once; Alloy assigns it to a solver suited to its material, couples the solvers inside every control step, and runs the scene in many parallel worlds on one GPU, or on a CPU. Every world carries a health grade, to help tell a failure of the physics from a failure of the policy. Alloy is built on Newton, MuJoCo Warp and Warp, and it is written to be driven by coding agents: its documentation ships inside the package, every error names its fix, and the engine is exposed as tools over the Model Context Protocol. In a cold test, agents that had never seen Alloy installed a pre-release from the package index and trained policies for walking, cable handling and pouring on a single GPU. We also report how throughput grows with the number of worlds, depth-camera throughput, agreement with closed-form references, and a reliability test over a thousand worlds.

items.title: Parsed, Plausible, Wrong: Output Format Controls Silent Errors in Small-Model Semantic Parsing
items.summary: A small fine-tuned parser that emits a well-formed but wrong tree fails silently: nothing downstream can tell. We ask whether the output format, a free design choice, controls how often this happens. On the PIZZA ordering benchmark we fine-tune two sub-billion models (Qwen3.5-0.8B and LFM2.5-350M) with LoRA on six lossless encodings of the same target tree, from 44.3 down to 10.9 tokens per order, including two…
items.abstract: A small fine-tuned parser that emits a well-formed but wrong tree fails silently: nothing downstream can tell. We ask whether the output format, a free design choice, controls how often this happens. On the PIZZA ordering benchmark we fine-tune two sub-billion models (Qwen3.5-0.8B and LFM2.5-350M) with LoRA on six lossless encodings of the same target tree, from 44.3 down to 10.9 tokens per order, including two matched-length pairs that vary surface form at fixed length. Across 300 runs (5 training pool sizes, 5 seeds) with a hierarchical bootstrap and Holm correction fixed before the results were read, shortening alone never helps, but writing the target in ordinary words does. The word encoding is the most accurate format on both models (87.5% vs. 85.8% exact match for the native s-expression on Qwen) while emitting 4.1x fewer tokens, and it cuts the silent error rate by 2.3x on Qwen and 1.8x on LFM2, separating at every pool size. Error analysis locates much of the gain in negation. All runs also learn to refuse off-menu input (held out: 95.9-99.0% handled) and to apply in-utterance self-corrections. Strict refusal has a measured price: 2.1-10.1% of real, mostly polite, orders are refused.

items.title: Interpreting Coding Agents Through Their Behavioral Trajectories
items.summary: Standard coding-agent benchmarks primarily evaluate binary task success, treating execution as a black box and obscuring the behaviors that produce those outcomes. We analyze a large corpus of 143,209 execution trajectories from 125 agent configurations spanning 117 unique models. To enable comparisons across heterogeneous agent interfaces, we develop a rule-based parser that maps raw execution traces to high-level…
items.abstract: Standard coding-agent benchmarks primarily evaluate binary task success, treating execution as a black box and obscuring the behaviors that produce those outcomes. We analyze a large corpus of 143,209 execution trajectories from 125 agent configurations spanning 117 unique models. To enable comparisons across heterogeneous agent interfaces, we develop a rule-based parser that maps raw execution traces to high-level actions such as repository search, file editing, and test execution, and audit its predictions against a six-model consensus reference on 500 events. We find that agents with similar solve rates can nevertheless differ substantially in how they explore, modify and verify code. Moreover, without using task outcomes, token counts, or tool names as features, aggregate behavioral profiles retrieve the corresponding agent stack across disjoint repository sets and programming languages, although task composition is not fully controlled in the cross-repository setting. Through analyses of frontier models and agent scaffolds, we further show that scaffold choice and reasoning effort systematically shift agents' search, editing, and testing behavior. We release the deterministic parser together with the full annotation and analysis pipeline alongside an annotated trajectory subset.

items.title: eDMD: Endpoint Distribution Matching for Few-Step Diffusion Distillation
items.summary: Distribution matching distillation (DMD) has emerged as a leading paradigm for distilling diffusion models into few-step students, where an auxiliary fake score model tracks the student's distribution and the discrepancy between the teacher and fake predictions drives the student toward the teacher. In multi-step distillation, although only the student's final output is delivered, existing methods train the fake…
items.abstract: Distribution matching distillation (DMD) has emerged as a leading paradigm for distilling diffusion models into few-step students, where an auxiliary fake score model tracks the student's distribution and the discrepancy between the teacher and fake predictions drives the student toward the teacher. In multi-step distillation, although only the student's final output is delivered, existing methods train the fake model on intermediate states or across all denoising steps. Consequently, the student's update signal becomes entangled with intermediate distributions, which can distort the matching direction and remain nonzero even after the student's final outputs already match the teacher distribution. To resolve this mismatch, we propose Endpoint Distribution Matching Distillation (eDMD), which trains a single shared fake model exclusively on the student's final outputs and uses it to correct every denoising step. Our theoretical analysis proves that this endpoint reference guarantees that the distribution matching term vanishes if and only if the student's final output distribution matches the teacher's, regardless of intermediate distributions. Beyond the fake reference, we further strengthen teacher supervision through a precise teacher (PT) that replaces single-step guided predictions with short multi-step trajectories on the final noise interval, paired with a calibrated query density for intermediate steps. Experiments on SD3-Medium, FLUX.2-klein (4B and 9B), and Qwen-Image-2.1 demonstrate that eDMD consistently outperforms existing distribution matching methods for 4-step generation.

items.title: Evidence-Governed Adoption of Self-Generated Updates in Autonomous AI Agents
items.summary: Autonomous agents modify prompts, memories, tools, workflows, and policies using interaction histories. Yet a plausible modification is not necessarily suitable for persistent adoption: candidate selection is adaptive, evaluators may be imperfect, and local gains can hide degradation against an earlier baseline. We introduce Evidence-Governed Evolution (EGE), a framework for governing adoption of self-generated…
items.abstract: Autonomous agents modify prompts, memories, tools, workflows, and policies using interaction histories. Yet a plausible modification is not necessarily suitable for persistent adoption: candidate selection is adaptive, evaluators may be imperfect, and local gains can hide degradation against an earlier baseline. We introduce Evidence-Governed Evolution (EGE), a framework for governing adoption of self-generated agent modifications. EGE separates candidate generation from confirmatory adoption, evaluates frozen candidates on fresh paired audits, requires meaningful improvement on a prespecified primary objective, protects declared capabilities through reference-relative non-inferiority tests, and applies governance constraints before bounded canary deployment. We establish an evaluator-calibrated simultaneous lower-bound construction for a countable sequence of adaptively generated candidates. It combines candidate-wise Hoeffding bounds with independent calibration samples comparing the operational evaluator with a prespecified reference procedure. We also formalise reference replacement through bridge tests, derive a cumulative degradation bound along a versioned reference lineage, and provide an audit-planning condition relating effect-size margin, sample sizes, and acceptance probability. A Monte Carlo stress test illustrates calibration under candidate-dependent evaluator optimism; it is a stylised statistical experiment, not an evaluation of a deployed agent. The guarantees are conditional on bounded paired scores, fresh sampling, a valid reference-evaluation construct, and declared evaluation distributions; they do not establish universal agent safety or robustness to arbitrary distribution shift.

items.title: When Expert Disagreement Hurts: Prestige and Selectivity in LLM Decision Revision
items.summary: When language models revise a decision after another agent disagrees, neither reversal counts nor final accuracy shows whether they are fixing mistakes or abandoning correct answers. We introduce a controlled two-pass audit that holds the question, the evidence, and the model's initial answer fixed and varies only the revision context: neutral reflection, anonymous disagreement, or disagreement attributed to a…
items.abstract: When language models revise a decision after another agent disagrees, neither reversal counts nor final accuracy shows whether they are fixing mistakes or abandoning correct answers. We introduce a controlled two-pass audit that holds the question, the evidence, and the model's initial answer fixed and varies only the revision context: neutral reflection, anonymous disagreement, or disagreement attributed to a domain expert. For binary decisions the accounting is exact: revision raises accuracy only if it is selective enough, reversing wrong answers more than a/(1-a) times as often as correct ones, where a is initial accuracy (nine times at 90%). Across five models and 1,989 evidence-grounded decisions in medicine, science, and law, no model clears this bar under expert disagreement, and accuracy falls by up to 16.1 points. The expert label, a prestige cue, adds reversals for four of the five models, yet its effect on accuracy ranges from a 5.2-point loss to a 2.4-point gain, so reversal counts are a poor proxy for harm. With identical arguments from both sources, the label still raises reversal for three proprietary models and in a pooled analysis of four newer models. Models also respond to stated source reliability. Revision pipelines should therefore be evaluated with paired, conditional metrics, per model and protocol.

items.title: Dataset Distillation via Drifting
items.summary: The task of dataset distillation concerns the learning of a small set of synthetic samples that can serve as an effective replacement for a large real dataset when used for downstream tasks. While many solutions have been proposed since the problem's inception, most of them primarily seek to optimize the distilled data with respect to a classifier. In this work, we propose a new distillation method that learns a set…
items.abstract: The task of dataset distillation concerns the learning of a small set of synthetic samples that can serve as an effective replacement for a large real dataset when used for downstream tasks. While many solutions have been proposed since the problem's inception, most of them primarily seek to optimize the distilled data with respect to a classifier. In this work, we propose a new distillation method that learns a set of samples such that they directly approximate the per-class data distribution. Specifically, we "drift" our distilled data in the latent space of a feature extractor such that they move both toward the real data and away from each other without using a classification objective. We find that our drifted data cover the real distribution significantly better than existing methods while still serving as powerful training samples for classification. Furthermore, we showcase our method's use as a visualization tool for better interpreting models and extend it beyond images to other modalities. Our work advances the frontier of dataset distillation, offering a novel synthesis method and proposing distribution-based metrics as a complementary evaluation. More broadly, our findings help address the growing need to understand both data and models by uncovering more about how they interact.

items.title: Unfinished-Bench: Measuring Rule Violations by Persistent Agents in Realistic Work Environments
items.summary: AI agents are increasingly equipped with persistence toward task completion to run delegated work autonomously for long periods, under many unstated constraints from internal documents and other people's authority. When completion requires violating a rule, the agent must decide alone, yet benchmarks of instruction-rule conflicts state the rule in the prompt or keep it hidden and do not evaluate persistence. We…
items.abstract: AI agents are increasingly equipped with persistence toward task completion to run delegated work autonomously for long periods, under many unstated constraints from internal documents and other people's authority. When completion requires violating a rule, the agent must decide alone, yet benchmarks of instruction-rule conflicts state the rule in the prompt or keep it hidden and do not evaluate persistence. We present Unfinished-Bench, a benchmark that gives models persistence in autonomous runs without a user, in realistic work environments with embedded rules. In each of its 97 scenarios across 7 organizations and 7 risk categories, the goal and the rule cannot both hold. We find that persistence raised violations of a rule in an internal document from 32.2% to 43.6%, five times the 8.5% for the same rule stated by the user. Of the document-rule violations, 98.3% occurred after the rule was displayed, and in 89% of a judged sample the agent first wrote down the rule. Violations of rules placed in the environment without user oversight can lead to serious incidents, so persistence-driven risks need to be evaluated. Benchmark documentation: https://francis21c.github.io/unfinished-bench/

items.title: Kezek: Splitting Mono Two-Person Conversations into Per-Speaker Tracks for Full-Duplex Dialogue Data
items.summary: Full-duplex spoken dialogue models learn turn-taking, overlaps and backchannels from conversations recorded with one channel per speaker, but most available conversational audio is a single mono mix. We present Kezek, a model that turns a mono recording of exactly two people into one track per person with the original length and timing; overlaps and short replies ("yeah", "mm-hm") stay on the track of the person who…
items.abstract: Full-duplex spoken dialogue models learn turn-taking, overlaps and backchannels from conversations recorded with one channel per speaker, but most available conversational audio is a single mono mix. We present Kezek, a model that turns a mono recording of exactly two people into one track per person with the original length and timing; overlaps and short replies ("yeah", "mm-hm") stay on the track of the person who said them. Kezek decides who speaks when and who is who once for the whole recording (stage 1: a two-voice activity model guided by a speaker fingerprint trained to be insensitive to phase), and a conditioned time-domain separator only carries out that decision (stage 2), with outputs that always sum to the input. Standard separation metrics miss the failures that matter for dialogue data, so we report short-reply retention, leakage onto the other person's solo, channel swaps and coverage. Against the open pipeline pyannote -> DialogueSidon on the same recordings, Kezek keeps more short replies (0.83 vs. 0.69 on Open Yap test; 0.80 vs. 0.71 over the other's speech on unseen telephone speech from CallHome English), mostly because it returns the whole recording while the external pipeline drops part of it (on the audio both return, reply retention is about the same: 0.859 vs. 0.865 on Open Yap); it also leaks less, swaps channels less often, and runs 4-5 times faster (about 230 hours of audio per GPU-hour). We also report negative results and an ideal-mask ceiling that locate the remaining gap: quiet replies under a louder voice. Code and weights are released under permissive licences.

items.title: LightTAR: Light and Fast Target-Aware Representations for Multimodal Tabular Learning
items.summary: Multimodal tabular learning involves classification and regression on tables combining structured numerical and categorical features with unstructured text and images. These unstructured fields are commonly represented by pretrained encoder embeddings reduced with principal component analysis (PCA). This reduction prioritizes input variance but may overlook information relevant to predicting the target. We introduce…
items.abstract: Multimodal tabular learning involves classification and regression on tables combining structured numerical and categorical features with unstructured text and images. These unstructured fields are commonly represented by pretrained encoder embeddings reduced with principal component analysis (PCA). This reduction prioritizes input variance but may overlook information relevant to predicting the target. We introduce LightTAR, a simple, inexpensive method that adapts dimensionality reduction to the prediction task. LightTAR augments the standard PCA representation with a few target-aware features extracted jointly from the final and an intermediate encoder layer using regularized partial least squares (PLS). We evaluate LightTAR with 21 tabular models, including tree ensembles, neural networks, and tabular foundation models. LightTAR improves average predictive performance for all models and, averaged across models, improves prediction on almost every MulTaBench dataset. These gains come with a small increase in total runtime relative to PCA representations. LightTAR integrates directly into existing encoding pipelines, improving tabular learners' predictive performance without modifying the encoder or the learner.

items.title: Duo: A Reciprocal World Model for Full-Duplex Interaction

items.abstract: In this report, we introduce the Reciprocal World Model (RWM) and present Duo v1, a full-duplex world model that continuously perceives audiovisual inputs while responding to users in real time. The RWM treats intelligence and physical reality as equally fundamental to what constitutes a world. Existing world models largely focus on simulating the latter, leaving reasoning and decision-making as external controls rather than intrinsic parts of the world itself. In RWM, we identify two equally fundamental capabilities: Intent, which provides the cognition underlying world interactions, and Realization, which generates coherent audio-visual behavior. To realize this formulation, Duo v1 introduces three key technical designs: (1) Leveraging autoregressive modeling for continuous interaction reasoning and participation decisions, rather than restricting it to instruction understanding for diffusion models. (2) Constructing chunk-specific conditions and synchronize tokens across Intent and Realization on a unified timeline. Module-specific attention masks enforce causal dependencies both within and across chunks, preventing access to future inputs. (3) Mitigating distribution shift in both modules through dual rollout distillation, training on autoregressively generated Intent tokens and synthesized audiovisual histories from Realization. Both modules continuously perceive real-time audio, video, and text, enabling full-duplex interaction with spontaneous conversations and interruptions. Beyond conversation, users can share real objects, reshape virtual scenes, guide assistants, or play audiovisual games without mouse or keyboard controls. The release of Duo v1 makes our first step, with the next version coming soon. We look forward to broader exploration of this emerging field.

items.abstract: Alveolar echinococcosis, caused by the parasite Echinococcus multilocularis, is a potentially lethal disease that requires the development of new medical treatments. Current drug screening methods depend on manual microscopy to count stained and unstained protoscoleces to determine viability, a process that is often slow and subject to human error. This study developed machine learning models to automate the classification of protoscolex survival to accelerate drug discovery. A total of 111 images containing 1,302 protoscoleces stained with eosin or methylene blue were analyzed. Histogram-based image features were extracted and subjected to preprocessing, dimensionality reduction, and feature selection. Six classification algorithms were trained using five-fold cross-validation and evaluated on internal test sets and an external validation set via receiver operating characteristic curve analysis. Results indicated that several models were highly effective, with internal test scores ranging from 0.8905 to 0.9467 and external validation scores between 0.7772 and 0.8214. Models based on support vector machine, logistic regression, and linear discriminant analysis demonstrated promising discriminatory performance across both internal and external datasets. The study concludes that machine learning can accurately and objectively classify the viability of protoscoleces based on stained images. This automated approach offers significant potential for standardizing high-throughput drug screening and facilitating the discovery of new therapeutics against this neglected zoonotic disease.

items.abstract: The scarcity of large, diverse, and unbiased protein–ligand binding datasets limits the performance of machine learning approaches in drug discovery, particularly for understudied proteins. The Target 2035 initiative aims to address this gap by generating open-access binding data for more than 2,000 human proteins, a goal whose value depends on maximizing the diversity of the selected targets. Because proteins with different folds can share chemically analogous binding sites, we reasoned that pocket similarity, rather than sequence or fold similarity, is the appropriate criterion for selecting representative targets that maximize coverage of the human pocketome. Here, we use PocketVec, an alignment-free descriptor of binding sites, to map the human globular pocketome, identifying 51,535 predicted druggable pockets across 15,559 proteins. A two-level hierarchical clustering, first within protein families and then across the whole proteome, grouped these pockets into 1,865 clusters of chemically similar binding sites. After discarding 533 clusters containing pockets with known ligands, we selected the 100 most populated of the remaining 1,332 ligand-free clusters and chose two high-quality representative pockets per cluster, ranked by their resemblance to known ligand-binding sites. Finally, we implemented two complementary prioritization strategies, one favoring structurally unexplored proteins and the other proteins amenable to experimental follow-up, and selected 200 pockets from 100 different clusters from each strategy, with 89 clusters in common. Both selections cover over 10,000 pockets in ∼5,600 proteins, approximately 36% of the human proteins with annotated druggable pockets, which represents a 2.8-to 4.4-fold increase in the number of covered pockets, domains, and proteins than random selection baselines. This pocket-based framework offers a principled strategy to select diverse targets for Target 2035 and other large-scale protein–ligand data generation efforts in chemical biology.

items.abstract: RNAs are emerging as promising therapeutic targets, and small-molecule binding can modulate their structure and function, creating opportunities for therapeutic development. Accurate identification of RNA–small-molecule binding sites is therefore important for understanding RNA–ligand interactions and facilitating RNA-targeted drug discovery. However, the structural complexity of RNA and the limited availability of experimentally characterized RNA–ligand complexes pose challenges for computational binding-site prediction. In this study, we propose RSMBind, a graph attention-based deep learning framework for nucleotide-level prediction of RNA–small-molecule binding sites. The model integrates geometric descriptors of the local three-dimensional environment with pretrained RNA language model embeddings to capture complementary structural and sequence information. We investigate three pretrained RNA language models—RNA-BERT, ERNIE-RNA and RNA-FM—and assess the contributions of sequence representations and geometric features through feature-level ablation experiments. The model is developed using the TR60 and HARIBOSS datasets and evaluated on four independent benchmark datasets: RB9, TE18, TL12 and JL10. RSMBind achieves the highest MCC among the compared methods on three of the four benchmarks, with relative improvements of 17.1% on RB9, 7.2% on TL12 and 16.0% on JL10 over the best previously reported results, while achieving competitive performance on TE18. Furthermore, RSMBind retains predictive capability when using only pretrained RNA language model embeddings, highlighting their potential utility when explicit tertiary structural features are unavailable. Structural analysis indicates differences in prediction performance across RNA structural regions, with loop-associated binding sites generally being captured more effectively than those embedded within stem regions. Additionally, 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations of selected RNA–ligand complexes provide insights into the relationship between predicted binding probabilities and dynamic ligand proximity, further highlighting the role of conformational dynamics in evaluating structure-based predictions. The source code is available at [ https://github.com/sharma-nandita/RSMBind ].

items.abstract: Customization and modification of machine learning derived sequences can be achieved by understanding the mechanics behind state-of-the-art protein design models such as ProteinMPNN. Uninterpretability is hypothesized to be due largely to polysemanticity where neural networks store more features than they have dimensions. Here, we introduce sparse autoencoders (SAEs) into ProteinMPNN which expand its latent space and uncovers correlations between the activations in sparse dimensions and the presence of protein features such as secondary structure, residue volume, residue shape, disulfide bridges, and coordination to ligands. Additionally, we show that sparse activations can be manipulated to produce a variant of the short chain variable fragment Brolucizumab that is more thermostable than variants produced by traditional machine learning methods based on high temperature molecular dynamics simulations. Thus, SAEs provide both mechanistic understanding of protein design models and allow customizable manipulation of sequence prediction.

items.abstract: Serpins (serine protease inhibitors) regulate proteolytic activity through a suicide-substrate inhibitory mechanism, whereby the serpin covalently traps and inactivates their target protease. Serpins are broadly conserved across eukaryotes, but the evolutionary and functional relationships between human SERPINE1, and Drosophila Serpins in incompletely defined. To identify candidate Drosophila functional analogs of SERPINE1/PAI-1, a multi-omics framework was applied to thoroughly compare the serpins across species. The multi-level analysis integrated orthology prediction, protein sequence and structural characterization, phylogenetic reconstruction, bulk tissue transcriptomics, single-cell transcriptomics, and aging-associated expression analysis. Candidate serpins (Spn42Da, Spn42Db, Spn42Dc, Spn42Dd, Spn28B, and Spn28F) were evaluated using DIOPT, AlphaFold/ChimeraX structural comparisons, reactive center loop analyses, phylogenetic distances, GTEx, Human Protein Atlas, FlyAtlas2, Fly Cell Atlas, and Aging Fly Cell Atlas datasets. Comparative analyses demonstrated full-length sequence and reactive center loop (RCL) divergence despite preservation of the canonical serpin fold. Tissue, cell-type, and age-associated expression analysis revealed distinct candidate-specific patterns. Spn42Dd comparisons uncovered similarities to human SERPINE1 in sequence/structural and broad expression but did not represent the strongest overall cross-species expression correlations. Spn42Da and Spn42Db received the highest cross species integrated support. Quality check of the ranking confirmed that Spn42Da and Spn42Db were stable top candidates across orthology, sequence alignment, and expression domains. The multi-domain analysis was unable to identify a single definitive Drosophila serpin as the closest counterpart to human SERPINE1, indicating that cross-species similarity is distributed across multiple candidate serpins. This study therefore provides a quantitative method for prioritizing potential evolutionary and functional analogs across highly divergent species.

items.abstract: Accurate, rapid, and standardized interpretation of multiparametric flow cytometry findings is essential for clinical decision-making in patients evaluated for suspected acute leukemia. This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of ChatGPT, a general-purpose large language model, in interpreting de-identified, laboratory-generated flow cytometry graphical outputs from patients with suspected acute leukemia and to assess its agreement with the consensus interpretation of two hematologists in terms of diagnostic classification, blast percentage estimation, and hematogone detection. This retrospective observational validation study included 560 patients who underwent bone marrow aspiration and flow cytometric immunophenotyping during their initial diagnostic evaluation for suspected acute leukemia. All included patients were undergoing initial diagnostic evaluation and had neither a previous diagnosis of leukemia nor prior leukemia-directed treatment. The consensus diagnosis established by two hematologists was considered the reference standard. Between May 4 and 15, 2026, de-identified, laboratory-generated PDF images containing flow cytometry dot plots from a three-tube acute leukemia panel comprising 28 antibody-fluorochrome combinations were uploaded directly through the ChatGPT Plus web interface and interpreted using GPT-5.5 (OpenAI). Raw FCS files were not provided. Using the same standardized prompt for each case, the model was asked to estimate the blast percentage, select a single most likely diagnosis from five predefined categories (no pathology, MDS, AML, B-ALL, or T-ALL), and determine the presence or absence of hematogones. The initial response for each case was archived and directly encoded without adjudication. Diagnosis-specific performance was evaluated using one-versus-rest sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value, accuracy, and F1-score. Overall agreement between ChatGPT-generated classifications and hematologist consensus was assessed using Cohen's kappa. Pearson's correlation coefficient was used to evaluate the association between blast percentage estimates, whereas Bland-Altman analysis was used to quantify agreement, systematic bias, and 95% limits of agreement. Hematogone detection was evaluated as a binary classification task using sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy. ChatGPT achieved an overall diagnostic accuracy of 78.8% (95% CI, 75.2%-81.9%), with substantial agreement with hematologist consensus (Cohen's κ = 0.712; 95% CI, 0.664-0.757). Diagnosis-specific sensitivity ranged from 69.2% to 87.3%, and PPV ranged from 60.0% to 93.5%. The highest sensitivity was observed for MDS, whereas the highest PPV was observed for no pathology. McNemar's test identified significant systematic differences between ChatGPT and hematologist classifications for no pathology (p = 0.041), AML (p = 0.008), and T-ALL (p = 0.023). Blast percentage estimates were strongly correlated (Pearson's r = 0.818; 95% CI, 0.789-0.844; p< 0.001); however, Bland-Altman analysis demonstrated a mean positive bias of 3.92 percentage points, indicating systematic overestimation by ChatGPT. For hematogone detection, ChatGPT achieved an accuracy of 89.5%, sensitivity of 70.3%, and specificity of 92.4%. ChatGPT-based flow cytometry interpretation showed promise for preliminary diagnostic classification and quality assurance applications. However, expert hematologist validation remains essential, particularly in scenarios associated with high diagnostic consequences, including AML and T-ALL classification, blast percentage estimation, and accurate discrimination of hematogones.

items.abstract: Integrating multimodal data is essential to advance neuroscience as a discipline. Large-scale collaborative efforts, exemplified by the BRAIN Initiative, together with advances in single-cell and spatial omics, multimodal imaging, human genetics, behavioral phenotyping, protein structure prediction, and related technologies, are transforming neuroscience into a data-rich, highly interconnected science. As experimental resources, scientific literature, and collaborative networks continue to expand, integrating discoveries across modalities, species, and levels of biological organization has become the field's central bottleneck. This Perspective argues that artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming essential for overcoming these constraints. Using six evolving approaches we outline strategies to accelerate AI adoption through community building and pilot projects that drive AI transformation at both the organizational and technological levels. Organizational transformation cultivates broad AI awareness and a pro-AI culture while technological transformation improves the efficiency, scalability, and quality of data analysis, allowing researchers to generate insights more rapidly and effectively. Together, these advances position AI as a key driver for advancing neuroscience at scale.

items.abstract: Intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) are central to many biological processes, but their function depends on dynamic conformational ensembles rather than a single structure. Despite the impact of artificial intelligence on protein structure prediction, determining these ensembles at atomistic resolution remains challenging. Recently, we introduced bAIes, a framework that leverages the structural information encoded in AlphaFold2 distograms to generate conformational ensembles of IDPs at atomistic resolution. Here, we extend this framework to six state-of-the-art structure prediction tools (AlphaFold2, AlphaFold3, Boltz-1, Boltz-2, ESMFold, and ESMFold2) and systematically compare the structural information encoded in their predicted inter-residue distance distributions. Despite differences between predictors, we show that bAIes generates ensembles with comparable accuracy against experimental NMR and SAXS data, and competitive performance relative to state-of-the-art all-atom simulations and alternative IDP ensemble generation methods. These results demonstrate that bAIes is robust to the choice of structure predictor and that the distance distributions generated by different deep learning architectures contain valuable information about the conformational preferences of disordered proteins. More broadly, our work highlights the potential of combining AI-derived structural information with physics-based modeling to generate atomistic ensembles of intrinsically disordered proteins and regions.

items.abstract: Molecular glues (MGs) modulate protein function by inducing or stabilizing protein interactions. However, accurately modeling MG ternary complexes remains challenging. Here, we present DiffTernary, a diffusion-based docking method for the joint prediction of relative protein arrangement and MG binding pose. We introduce Ternary-PDB, a dataset of 76,702 experimentally determined ternary complexes curated from the Protein Data Bank using structural filters and a release cutoff aligned with AlphaFold 3 (AF3). When trained on this dataset, DiffTernary achieved acceptable protein-protein interaction (PPI) predictions (DockQ > 0.23) for 50.0% of MGBench complexes with a single prediction, compared with 51.1% for AF3. In comparisons with AF3, OpenFold3, ESMFold2, Protenix-v1 and Protenix-v2, DiffTernary ranked second with a best-of-25 PPI prediction success rate of 78.4%, behind ESMFold2 (90.9%) and ahead of AF3 (72.7%). A separate DiffTernary model trained on TernaryDB achieved a mean DockQ of 0.306 on the 94 complexes in the TernaryDB MGD test set with a single prediction, compared with 0.228 for DeepTernary. Confidence-based selection among 40 samples yielded acceptable PPI predictions for 41.5% of complexes, compared with 30.9% for DeepTernary. An E2Former variant increased training and sampling throughput 6.90-fold and 4.37-fold, respectively, under the evaluated configurations. Together, DiffTernary and Ternary-PDB provide an efficient docking approach for MG complex prediction and a valuable structural resource for MG discovery and design.

items.abstract: Abstract Inorganic polyphosphate (polyP) can alter protein function through noncovalent binding, yet its partners among human membrane associated proteins remain poorly characterized. PolyP is recognized through two modes: a structure-based mode driven by charge complementarity with sites assembled by protein folding, and a more recently defined sequence-based mode at histidine and lysine rich tracts. The sequence determinant is well defined and directly searchable; the structure-based mode has few characterized examples and no systematic search method, because its residues leave no contiguous sequence signature. Broad experimental binding screens are especially demanding for integral membrane proteins, which require specialized conditions. We therefore developed a computational workflow that searches predicted structures for surfaces able to accommodate a phosphate chain. We designed custom scores that integrate surface electrostatics, docking results and structural confidence to prioritize candidates. From 19,481 completed docking searches on 5,648 AlphaFold models representing 2,925 UniProt protein entries, we nominated 82 entries as candidates for noncovalent polyP binding. Predicted polyP contacts in 18 candidate entries overlapped experimentally characterized functional residues, linking the predicted interfaces to established sites of ligand recognition, regulation and membrane attachment. The workflow ranks computational results rather than measuring binding, providing specific targets for experimental investigation.

items.abstract: Sepsis constitutes a life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. SESN2 (sestrin 2), an evolutionarily conserved stress-responsive protein, is a pivotal regulator of cellular homeostasis. Here, we identified TRIM13 (tripartite motif-containing 13) as a regulator that modulated the stability of SESN2 at the post-translational level. Specifically, TRIM13 promoted K63-linked ubiquitination of SESN2 with subsequent upregulation of its functional activation. Ubiquitinated SESN2 initiated a selective macroautophagic/autophagic program that facilitated the recruitment of SQSTM1/p62 (sequestosome 1/p62) to mitochondrial surfaces. The enhanced interaction between ubiquitinated SESN2 and the mitophagy receptor FUNDC1 (FUN14 domain-containing 1) at mitochondria-associated membranes (MAMs), facilitated by this modification, potentiated the mitophagic clearance of damaged mitochondria. In addition, it inhibited the interaction between FUNDC1 and RIPK3 (receptor-interacting serine-threonine kinase 3), which in turn ameliorated dysfunction and necroptosis of dendritic cells (DCs) upon sepsis. Thus, our findings establish that TRIM13 mitigates septic responses by activating SESN2-mediated mitophagy through ubiquitination, offering new insights into potential immunomodulatory strategies for sepsis. items.abstract: The twenty-first century has transformed longevity research through genomics, epigenomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, microbiome science, digital phenotyping and artificial intelligence. Yet healthy longevity remains difficult to explain because its determinants are commonly studied as separate molecular layers, mechanisms or biomarkers. Here, we introduce Longevitomics as an integrative systems framework for understanding, modeling and predicting healthy longevity and define the Longevitome inspired by the Latin expression vita longa (long life) as the dynamic architecture of biological, environmental and behavioral determinants that collectively shape psychosomatic resilience across the life course. We position this proposal in relation to the Hallmarks of Aging, geroscience, biological-age biomarkers, multi-omics and systems medicine. Longevitomics is not intended to replace these established frameworks or to constitute another molecular "ome." Rather, it provides a systems-level framework in which mechanistic hallmarks, multi-omic layers, physiological phenotypes, exposures and adaptive responses can be integrated longitudinally. We further consider how network analysis, causal inference, machine learning and digital-twin approaches may enable reconstruction of individual Longevitome trajectories and support a transition toward predictive and personalized longevity medicine.

items.abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) has established that gene expression is driven by stochastic transcriptional bursting. However, inferring burst dynamics from static scRNA-seq snapshots is fundamentally constrained by parameter unidentifiability and model topology mismatch. Here, we propose PhysInfer, an unsupervised framework that integrates a physics-constrained neural network with adaptive model selection and parameter decoupling. A physics-informed loss function, combining stationary-distribution likelihood with zero-count anchoring, reparameterizes the optimization from unidentifiable microscopic rates to an interpretable macroscopic burst-quantity representation of burst size and burst frequency, thereby providing an interpretable parameterization for assessing practical recoverability in static data. Validation on synthetic data with known ground-truth parameters confirms high inference accuracy in low-to-medium activation regimes and shows that recovery of BS and productive BF becomes increasingly condition-dependent as the ON-state probability approaches saturation; under different recovery criteria, the condition-specific upper Pon limit for simultaneously recovering BS and productive BF varies with cell number and capture efficiency. Applied to a mouse embryonic fibroblast (MEF) dataset, PhysInfer reconstructs a transcriptional dynamic manifold across the 2,137-gene secondary BIC analysis set, showing cross-gene variation in fitted burst frequency and burst size. A model-specific stationary likelihood combined with zero-count anchoring improves robustness to zero-heavy observations. The adaptive topology module further identifies a distinct subset of genes with stable support for an effective sequential 3-state representation, revealing distributional structure beyond that captured by standard 2-state fitting. PhysInfer thus provides a robust, topology-adaptive, and interpretable solution for characterizing transcriptional kinetic patterns from static single-cell transcriptomic snapshots.

items.abstract: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is associated with poor outcomes, with 5-year survival after hospitalisation as low as 35-40%. Despite its growing prevalence, effective treatments remain limited. A major barrier to therapeutic success is the substantial biological and clinical heterogeneity within HFpEF, suggesting that distinct patient profiles may require different management strategies. This study investigates whether graph-based machine learning methods can identify distinct patient clusters within the HFpEF population and assess their relationships with clinical characteristics and outcomes. We analysed a multimodal dataset of 133 symptomatic HFpEF patients, comprising more than 240 K attributes derived from comprehensive cardiovascular assessment. These included cardiac MRI, echocardiography, circulating biomarkers of fibro-inflammation, and high-resolution proteomics. Five conventional unsupervised clustering methods were first applied but failed to produce clinically coherent groups, largely due to the complexity and multimodality of the data. To address this, we implemented a minimally supervised Graph Neural Network (GNN) that incorporated limited label information while modelling relationships between patients. This approach produced five clusters with potential clinical relevance. Importantly, cluster membership remained significantly associated with survival after adjustment for established clinical risk factors, including age, sex, BNP levels, symptom burden, and kidney function. Internal validation yielded an accuracy of 0.706 and an $F1$-score of 0.613, indicating reasonably consistent performance and suggesting that graph structure may aid generalisation and class-wise prognostic prediction. Overall, the findings show that minimally supervised graph-based learning can more effectively capture the underlying structure of multimodal HFpEF data than traditional methods. Visualisation and cluster quality metrics further support the effectiveness of the GNN approach.

items.abstract: Abstract Background Bisphenol A (BPA) is a high-production-volume endocrine-disrupting chemical, and meningioma is a common hormone-sensitive intracranial tumour. A systematic, reproducible molecular map linking BPA-responsive genes to meningioma transcriptomes has been lacking. We therefore developed a fully computational pipeline that integrates multi-cohort transcriptomics, chemical–target databases, nested machine learning, single-cell localisation and molecular docking to prioritise candidate markers while treating all docking and classification outputs as computational evidence rather than clinical causality. Results Three GEO microarray cohorts (GSE43290, GSE54934, GSE84263; 165 tumours, 23 normals) were merged on 10,938 genes after ComBat correction. Differential expression (682 DEGs) and WGCNA tumour modules (153 genes) were intersected with BPA targets from SwissTargetPrediction (96), SEA (19), PharmMapper (174), CTD and ChEMBL (five-source union 2,250) and meningioma genes from Open Targets/CTD. Twenty-five BPA-responsive core candidates emerged; consensus PPI×SHAP hubs were ACTA2 , BMP4 , FLNA and FLNB (Table 2 ranks 7.0 / 12.0 / 13.0 / 12.0). Nested tumour-versus-normal classifiers approached a performance ceiling (best external AUC 1.000; 83/109 models = 1.0), interpreted cautiously under class imbalance, whereas WHO-grade prediction was weak (external AUC ≤ 0.677). In GSE183655, BMP4 / FLNB mapped to tumour mesenchymal cells and ACTA2 to pericyte/smooth-muscle niches. AutoDock Vina affinities were weaker at hubs (− 5.17 to − 5.70 kcal/mol) than at ESR1 / ESR2 / PTGS2 (− 8.21 to − 8.49), with symmetry-aware redock RMSDs supporting control-site validity. Conclusions This reproducible pipeline provides computational evidence that cytoskeletal and BMP genes mark meningioma tissue within a BPA-responsive intersection. Direct high-affinity BPA–hub binding is not supported relative to classical oestrogen receptors and PTGS2 . Wet-lab and exposure-linked studies are required before translational inference.

items.abstract: Pancreaticojejunostomy (PJ) leak after pancreatoduodenectomy is graded by the International Study Group of Pancreatic Surgery (ISGPS) postoperative pancreatic fistula (POPF) definition, which captures clinical relevance but not the anatomical target to be treated. This structured narrative review examines endoscopic management of PJ leak and dehiscence and proposes complementary, computed tomography (CT)-informed phenotypes: biochemical leak without an actionable target (Phenotype 1); persistent external fistula without a drainable collection (Phenotype 2); drainable collection with preserved apposition (Phenotype 3); and complete loss of PJ apposition (Phenotype 4), subdivided by remnant perfusion (4a/4b). These phenotypes are hypothesis-generating and unvalidated. The corresponding objectives are observation, fistula internalization, collection source control and pancreatic diversion. Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS)-guided drainage, transanastomotic and pancreatic-duct interventions, lumen-apposing metal stents, rendezvous and vacuum-based techniques should be integrated with interventional radiology and surgery according to anatomy and physiological stability, after delayed haemorrhage has been excluded or controlled. Evidence on reconstruction technique, operative approach, stents, drains, risk scores, radiomics and artificial intelligence is also summarized: none removes the need for structured surveillance, and no prediction tool yet addresses structural dehiscence. Evidence is largely retrospective. Prospective studies should test whether combining ISGPS grade, CT-defined anatomy and microbiology improves selection for minimally invasive rescue.

items.abstract: BackgroundOutcomes after acute ischemic stroke (AIS) vary beyond lesion burden and clinical severity, suggesting a role for baseline structural brain vulnerability. We evaluated whether brain age gap (BrainAGE) derived from routine non-contrast computed tomography (NCCT) is associated with functional outcome after AIS.MethodsWe analyzed 1,173 AIS patients from a prospective multicenter cohort. A deep learning model estimated brain age from contralesional baseline NCCT to minimize lesion-related confounding. BrainAGE was defined as predicted minus chronological age. The primary outcome was 90-day functional status, assessed using proportional odds regression adjusted for age, sex, baseline stroke severity, early ischemic changes, and reperfusion therapy.ResultsBrainAGE was higher in AIS patients than in controls (+3.1 ± 9.1 years; p<0.001). Higher BrainAGE was associated with worse functional outcome after adjustment for age, sex, and other clinical predictors (POR 1.091 per 5 years; 95% CI 1.023-1.162; p=0.008). BrainAGE improved model fit but modestly improved discrimination.ConclusionsBrainAGE from routine NCCT provided modest incremental prognostic information beyond age and conventional clinical predictors. These findings support CT-based BrainAGE as a marker of brain health complementary to established prognostic factors. Whether BrainAGE improves patient-level risk stratification or clinical decision-making requires independent external validation and prospective evaluation.

items.abstract: Cardiovascular diseases continue to be the primary cause of mortality worldwide; however, precise diagnosis is often limited by dependence on individual data modalities and the unclear nature of traditional deep learning models. In this study, we introduce an explainable multimodal deep learning framework that simultaneously analyzes cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and structured clinical variables through a bidirectional cross-modal attention mechanism that operates on token sequences. The architecture utilizes modality-specific encoders ResNet-50 for imaging and a multilayer perceptron for clinical data interconnected through attention that dynamically aligns complementary information, reducing feature dilution and modal dominance. A multitask objective that includes classification, contrastive alignment (InfoNCE), and regularization further reinforces semantic consistency across modalities. Integrated post hoc explainability modules, such as Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping for spatial localization and SHapley Additive exPlanations for clinical feature attribution, offer transparent decision support. Tested on a cohort of 12,847 patients using fivefold cross-validation, the framework achieved an accuracy of 94.2% and an area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve of 0.97, significantly surpassing unimodal and traditional multimodal baselines (p < 0.01). The explanations generated showed 91% concordance with independent cardiologist evaluations. The findings presented herein were derived through internal five-fold cross-validation conducted at a solitary tertiary care institution, thereby substantiating internal validity while limiting multicenter generalizability; consequently, external validation is requisite for broader applicability. These results demonstrate that attention-driven multimodal fusion, combined with post hoc explainability, provides both strong diagnostic performance and clinically useful transparency, positioning the framework as a promising internally validated approach and a foundation for future external validation.

items.abstract: Background O-(2-[18F]fluoroethyl)-L-tyrosine positron emission tomography ([ 18 F]FET PET) is clinically useful in neuro-oncology but limited by cost and availability. We assessed the clinical utility of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-derived synthetic [ 18 F]FET PET. Methods A total of 489 patients with histologically confirmed gliomas or brain metastases were retrospectively analyzed. A deep learning model generated synthetic PET images from multimodal MRI in the overall cohort and subgroups. Synthetic PET was evaluated against reference PET for image similarity by peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and structural similarity index (SSIM), standardized uptake value ratio (SUVR) analysis by Pearson correlation and Bland-Altman analysis, and blinded reader assessment for glioma grading and high-grade glioma (HGG) versus solitary brain metastasis (SBM) differentiation using receiver operating characteristic analysis with area under the curve (AUC). Results Synthetic PET showed high similarity to reference PET in the overall, glioma, and metastasis groups (PSNR, 34.7-35.5 dB; SSIM, 0.90-0.96), and SUVR correlations were strong (r = 0.77-0.93, all P < 0.001), with minimal bias and narrow limits of agreement. Compared with MRI alone, MRI with synthetic PET improved glioma grading and HGG-SBM differentiation, increasing AUC from 0.815 to 0.941 and from 0.816 to 0.901 for glioma grading and from 0.731 to 0.871 and from 0.784 to 0.872 for HGG-SBM differentiation across the 2 readers (all P < 0.05). No significant differences were found between MRI with synthetic and reference PET for either task (all P > 0.05). Conclusions MRI-derived synthetic [ 18 F]FET PET may enhance glioma grading and HGG-SBM differentiation, providing a PET-like alternative when FET PET is unavailable.

items.abstract: Rationale and objectives Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a disease that is difficult to diagnose because its clinical findings are nonspecific and it carries high mortality when not treated early. Computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA), the gold standard for diagnosis, cannot be performed in every patient because of contraindications related to contrast medium; Noncontrast computed tomography (NCCT), on the other hand, cannot be used as a reliable tool for exclusion because of its low sensitivity. Materials and methods In this retrospective study, the paired images of 716 patients (129 PE-positive, 587 PE-negative) who had undergone both CTPA and NCCT on the same day between 2018 and 2026 were examined. The availability of two scans obtained from the same patient on the same day provided a paired cohort in which clinical and anatomical variables other than the presence of contrast were largely held constant, so that the CTPA scan established with certainty where a thrombus lay in each patient whose noncontrast scan was analyzed. Each scan was converted into a 12-second mediastinal-window video, from which a 40-frame segment centered on the temporal midpoint of the recording was extracted for analysis. For the automatic detection of thrombus, three-dimensional deep learning architectures have been developed: PureStream-3D, BiLSTM-ResNet-3D based on bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM), and AttnFocus-3D based on an attention mechanism. The models have been optimized with different training configurations to address class imbalance, and the dataset has been divided at the patient level into 70% training, 20% validation, and 10% independent test sets. Results In the CTPA test set, the highest discrimination has been achieved by the AttnFocus-3D-1 model (accuracy 0.9306; area under the curve [AUC] 0.98), whereas the most balanced sensitivity-specificity profile has been obtained with the BiLSTM-ResNet-3D-2 variant (sensitivity 0.9138, specificity 0.8571). In the NCCT test set, the AttnFocus-3D-2 architecture has reached an accuracy of 0.9306, an AUC of 0.97, a sensitivity of 0.9655, and a specificity of 0.7857. Conclusion Taken together, these findings indicate that the developed deep learning approaches are strong in confirming the presence or absence of PE and can be considered as a decision-support infrastructure in clinical scenarios with high diagnostic uncertainty.

items.abstract: Early identification and staging of Alzheimer's disease (AD) require integrated assessment of amyloid deposition, tau pathology, and neurodegeneration. PET provides spatially resolved in vivo imaging biomarkers, but its routine use is constrained by cost, tracer availability, and radiation exposure, limiting access to complete A/T/N imaging profiles. We propose a conditional flow matching-based framework that estimates SUV-space PET-derived phenotypes related to 18 F-FDG, 18 F-florbetapir and 18 F-flortaucipir from a single T1-weighted MRI scan. To address limitations in SUV-level quantitative fidelity, single-tracer applicability, and external generalization, the framework combines a PET prior network with a time-conditioned velocity network and uses multi-constraint losses to preserve SUV accuracy, regional uptake consistency, and anatomical boundaries. The model was developed using 1,978 paired ADNI MRI-PET records from 991 participants and evaluated in a predefined ADNI test set and an independent hospital PET/MR cohort of 514 participants. In ADNI, voxel-level MAEs were 0.012, 0.034, and 0.021 SUV, with representative ROI Pearson correlations of 0.978, 0.842, and 0.781. In the hospital cohort, corresponding MAEs were 0.014, 0.037, and 0.024 SUV, with ROI correlations of 0.952, 0.803, and 0.834. In OASIS, generated PET-derived features improved CDR stratification and future cognitive decline prediction, increasing AUCs from 0.662 to 0.739 and from 0.569 to 0.643. These findings suggest that the method can provide PET-derived phenotypes related to A/T/N analysis from structural MRI when PET is unavailable, but should not be interpreted as a replacement for molecular PET assessment.

items.abstract: Study DesignDiagnostic accuracy study.ObjectiveTo determine whether a general-purpose multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) model, Gemini 3 Pro, grades lumbar neuroforaminal stenosis on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in agreement with expert radiologists, particularly for severe stenosis, and whether a vertebral-level localizer overlay helps.MethodsOne hundred lumbar MRIs from the Radiological Society of North America (RSNA) 2024 Lumbar Spine Degenerative Classification Dataset, graded by expert radiologists, provided 1,000 foramina (five levels, both sides) labeled normal/mild, moderate, or severe. Sagittal and axial T2-weighted series were converted into short scrolling videos and submitted to the model with a structured grading prompt; no task-specific training was performed. The primary outcome was agreement with expert grades (linearly weighted Cohen's kappa, κw); secondary outcomes were accuracy, severe-stenosis sensitivity, direction of errors, and the localizer effect.ResultsAgreement with expert grading was poor (κw 0.20, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.14-0.26). Accuracy was 70.6% (95% CI 67.7-73.4) but reflected the 70.4% of foramina that were normal/mild. The model identified 17.9% of severe foramina (95% CI 8.9-30.4) and called 58.9% normal/mild. Errors were systematically toward undergrading (p < 0.001). The localizer did not improve accuracy (70.0% vs 70.6%, p = 0.590) and reduced severe sensitivity (3.6% vs 17.9%, p = 0.043).ConclusionsWithout task-specific training, a general-purpose AI model reached moderate accuracy only because most foramina were normal or mild; it missed most severe stenosis and systematically undergraded. In its current form this approach is unsuitable for screening, triage, operative decision-making, or independent report generation.

items.abstract: Medical imaging is essential for diagnosing disease, guiding treatment and monitoring patients over time. Although artificial intelligence has advanced image interpretation, existing medical models often address restricted tasks, while general-purpose proprietary models lack access to private clinical imaging required to achieve medical expertise. Developing models that can interpret complex examinations and communicate their findings in the context of clinical decisions remains a major challenge. Here, we show that Neuro-VL, a vision-language model trained on nearly one million neuroimaging studies from routine clinical care, can interpret complete imaging examinations and engage in natural language conversations about their findings. Across internal and international datasets, Neuro-VL outperformed frontier general-purpose and specialized medical models in diagnosing, localizing, and describing abnormalities, as well as generating comprehensive radiology reports. The model also compared serial examinations to assess disease progression and more reliably resisted misleading clinical assumptions than leading frontier models from OpenAI and Google. These results extend health system learning beyond individual predictions to interactive image interpretation and longitudinal disease monitoring. They demonstrate how the collective clinical experience of health systems can be used to develop medical AI with specialized expertise and broad clinical capabilities.

items.abstract: GPT-6 Astra can drive a robot arm directly through a fixed harness, and scores of such robot-use agents on RoboDojo have risen quickly since. Reported systems differ in harness and test subset and often change several designs at once, so it is hard to tell which choices produce the gains. We take these designs apart and test them in one framework, along the harness around the model, the action interface, the reuse of experience and the scene geometry given to the model. A lean harness that keeps the full episode history and stops each motion early goes a long way. Reusing experience changes how the model acts but is not a free lunch, and scene geometry helps most, even when depth is predicted from RGB alone. JustRUA starts from the official L3 harness and keeps only what matters most. Even with no learned policy, self-improvement loop or task-specific tuning, this simple harness raises the score on the RoboDojo simulation benchmark substantially, from 29.7 to 50.3.
